content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

The stage is set (by designer James Morgan) at the WIRT Radio Station in 1946; carols and songs of the era are sung as the cast of characters (an ensemble of 5) enter the station’s recording room, peppering their voices into ‘Let it Snow,’ insinuating that the weather outside is “frightful” on this Christmas Eve.  But all is warm and merry inside, as a pianist underscores the live radio recording of It’s A Wonderful Life, the classic film by Frank Capra, released in the same year.

The story is well known and loved, a rewatch for many each holiday season, and serves as a beautiful end-of-year parable for how even the smallest of lives can have such a large impact on those around them.  This retelling honors the era of the film with its 1940s design (costumes by David Toser and properties by Nicole Rozanski add to this effect) and the story is retold with classic foley-style sound effects (coupled with supporting audio design by Florian Staab) as the actors embody the citizens of Bedford Falls through four central microphones.

The audience too is cast to play their part as the live studio audience for the radio recording, asked to playfully participate through large “ON AIR” and “APPLAUSE” lights at the front of the stage.  

Fans of the movie will be pleased and enjoy this adaptive retelling. The ensemble cast bring energy and heart to the story, embodying a variety of characters and incorporating classic songs of the era and cheeky commercial recordings between acts. 

Rufus Collins provides a strong base narrative to the piece as the heavenly angel charging Clarence (played with comedy and energy by Ashley Robinson) to help George Bailey (Reed Lancaster).  Lancaster embodies a 1940s tone in his performance, leaning heavily into the restraint of Bailey’s character, but bringing in depth of emotion around his realization that his life has meaning.  Ali Ewoldt absolutely shines as Mary Bailey, bringing sheer joy to the stage with every scene, and Leenya Rideout embodies all ages and temperaments with believability.

A solid performance that is sure to leave guests feeling lighter and eager to embody the holiday spirit, It’s A Wonderful Life: A Live Radio Play is a great way to spend an afternoon or evening around the holidays and a wonderful retelling of the classic Christmas parable.

 

ITS A WONDERFUL LIFE: A LIVE RADIO PLAY – by Anthony E. Palermo; directed by Charlotte Moore

[adapted for radio from Frank Capra’s 1946 film, based on the story ‘The Greatest Gift’ by Philip Van Doren Stern]

FEATURING – Rufus Collins; Ali Ewoldt; Reed Lancaster; Leenya Rideout; Ashley Robinson

Scenic design by James Morgan; costume design by David Toset; lighting design by Michael Gottlieb; sound design by Florian Staab; properties by Nicole Rozanski.  Presented by Irish Repertory Theatre: Charlotte Moore, artistic director; Ciarán O’Reilly, producing artistic director.  Thru December 31 at Francis J. Greenburger Mainstage (132 West 22nd Street, New York, NY 10011.)

title.rendered: Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York)

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) is a story about a wide-eyed Brit who only knows the city through movies and a jaded New Yorker who go on a wedding adventure. It’s delightful. Their play and discovery of each other is funny and charming as the two characters get to know each other, slowly revealing their personal pain, and finding solace in the discovery.

Dougal’s dad, 57, abandoned he and his mom in England before he was born to go to the states. He became a millionaire but didn’t keep up contact. They’ve never met but Dougal’s been invited to a wedding. The wedding is of Mark, Dougal’s dad, to Robin’s sister Melissa, 30, who Robin is on the skids with. Robin’s assigned task is to meet Dougal at the airport and bring him to his hotel. Mission accomplished she heads home before work the next day. Next day she volunteers to go pick up the cake for the wedding and Dougal worms his way into that adventure where they discover more about each other and reveal more about each other’s lives.

It’s kind of a romcom, buddy adventure story all rolled into one. There are a number of plot twists and reveals that takes watching the whole showto the end in order to put the pieces together. It’s their fractured families that they’ve grown up in that has them both lost as to who they really are. They find themselves a little better informed getting to know each other.

Sam Tutty plays the 25-year-old Englishman Dougal Todd with such a wide eyed puppy dog quality (“a golden retriever but actually less boundaried”) and immediately wins the audience to his wonderment of life and enchantment of New York City. Christiani Pitts is the 26-year-old New Yorker Robin Rainey who is jaded to what life has become for her and only begrudgingly opens up to Dougal who brings a new perspective to her life. Neither of them has much money but abscond with Mark’s credit card (that they used to pay for the $2000 wedding cake) and end up having a night on the town (“I pity the rich. They’ll never know what it’s like to be rich for only one night.”).

The play begins at JFK. Soutra Gilmour’s set is composed of a mound of suitcases affixed to a turntable on stage. Throughout the show they change, fold and flip open to become a Chinatown restaurant, an Uber, a fancy cocktail spot, an ice skating rink, the Bump and Grind coffee shop, the Plaza Hotel, a subway, and various streets in Manhattan and Brooklyn. The play is a romcom about New York City as well, seen from the first time and from the viewpoint of someone who’s lived there her whole life.

This would be a thumbs up date night show no matter your age.

——-

Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) was written by Jim Barne and Kit Buchan, directed by Tim Jackson.

Cast: Christiani Pitts and Sam Tutty.

Set and Costume Designer, Soutra Gilmour; Lighting Designer, Jack Knowles; Sound Designer, Tony Gayle; Orchestrations, Lux Pyramid;  Hair, Wig, and Makeup design, Cheryl Thomas; Associate Director and Choreographer, Asmeret Ghebremichael.

Longacre Theatre, 220 W. 48th St., New York

Tickets can be had HERE.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

I feel as though I am the one person on the planet who has never heard Ann Kittredge.

Silly me.  THAT is about to change.

Kittredge is a treasure and a pleasure.  This is evidenced by her performance which is flawless: a soprano who fills her voice with color and vibrancy.  Her generosity and popularity are also evidenced by the many, many guests who donated their talents to this performance on December 3 at Chelsea Table + Stage.  Karen Mason got thing started after Kittredge welcomed us with story and song.  Mason gave us a code red version of “Santa Claus is Coming to Town”, waking us out of a winter slow down and rocketing us smack into the rafters. Mason was was followed by her talented husband/composer, Paul Rolnick, singing one of his own compositions, “It’ll Be Christmas Before You Know It (I have always been a fine of composers singing their own songs – Irving Berlin and Stephen Sonheim come to mind – and Rolnick did not disappoint).  Other extraordinary talents included Brent Barrett who sand a song, “Christmas Mornings” written at top speed by his husband, Bernard Blanks. Jeff Harner gave us a sweet rendition of “The Little Drummer Boy“.  Both he and Barrett followed up their solos with duets with Kittredge that were perfection.

In addition to singers, Kittredge welcomed musical directors to the piano.  In particular there was  Alex Rybeck accompanied Kittredge on the song “Snow” made famous by Bing Crosby in the film “White Christmas.”  What none of us knew was that this early composition by Irving Berlin started out life as “Free” in the musical “Call Me Madam” but was cut because it was too controversial.  Originally it was called “Free” and the opening lyrics are

Free.  The only thing I want/upon this earth is to be Free.

You see, Kittredge is not jus a pretty face – she is a marvel of a messenger.  You can listen to the song here: https://youtu.be/8vIhvEf8dRI – I cannot find it anywhere else on the web.  But it is a Cold War Gem that is sadly applicable today.

All in all it was a stellar evening that, in case  you were not feeling full of whatever holiday is your fancy, will provide the warmth and spice and reassurance that we don’t notice is missing until it shows up.

Mention MUST be made of the trio backing Kittredge: Musical Director Christopher Denny on piano,  who doubled as lyric coach when needed, Mary Ann McSweeny on bass and Rex Benincasa on drums.  The evening was directed by Barry Kleinbort.

This show was a celebration of Kittredge’s newest album “You Sleigh Me.” You would not go wrong grabbing this one to give to a chum who loves beautiful music and will appreciate theses tunes as a light in on our collective path.

The Album is produced by award-winning songwriter and record producer Paul Rolnick, and will be available on all digital platforms. For more information, visit www.jazzheads.com

Be on the lookout for Kittredge – she will be back!!!

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

If you know a nurse, or have seen a nurse in person or in the movies, or know what a nurse is, or read about nurses – any or all of the above – DIVERSION is a play for you.  Full stop.

To cut to the chase: “Diversion” is the noun for what happens when prescription drugs in a controlled setting are diverted. When they do not stay on their intended path and go missing.  In this case the afore-mentioned drug is opioids, and the suspected culprits are part of a very tight knit group of nurses who are working the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) at an unspecified hospital.  ICU is what it sounds like.  It is a unit filled with crises, dangerous circumstances, life and death.  This is the norm for these nurses.  Tell them they are suspects in a diversion and the stakes go up a bazillion percent.

As in all well written plays the subject at hand is not the subject at hand.  It is not the opioids.  It is the people affected by the ripple effect of them having gone missing.  Bess (Thaïs Bass-Moore) is at the top of the food chain.  She is the supervisor. Whatever happens is on her.  The resident nurses are left to circle and speculate. To point fingers when no one is watching.  Where author Scott Organ excels is in his refusal to take sides, to put his hand on the scales.  Thus we are given the opportunity to go deep instead of wide and experience what makes these people tick.

West Duchovny and Tricia Alexandro; photo by Edward T. Morris

Fortunately Organ is blessed by an astonishing cast who take the word “ensemble” seriously.  It would be fun to try and single out one actor who takes the lead, but that would be a waste of time. Tricia Alexandro as Emelia bears the weight of a profession she loves that is also wearing her down to the nubbins. Colleen Clinton as Josephine, a former nurse now a consultant, is a woman who cannot afford to dip her toe into old waters – or at least act like she is immune.  West Duchovny (Mandy) is the New Kid in Town who wants to balance her passion for this difficult career with her wild and sketchy life out there. DeAnna Lenhart (Amy) shares experience with Emelia and buries it under a gruff exterior that hides a generous heart.  Connor Wilson (Mike) is a more or less single dad whose son has unspecified behavioral issues and whose partner is mostly MIA. Mike is on a short tether that he minds carefully – it is all about balance.

The story line bounces back and forth seamlessly between these characters and, thanks to the actors’ skill, a terrific script and thoughtful direction by Scott Barrish, we are guided through a tunnel that most of us would forgo if given the opportunity.  Yes, the mystery is solved.  Yes we do not see it coming.

And yes we are the beneficiaries of the tale.  We get to climb inside these people and experience what we could heretofore not imagine.

Now we can.

Here is how this shakes out: The Barrow Group created this gift.  In order for it to work, the gift must be accepted.

That is where we come in.  We complete the circle.  And “Diversion” is one helluva circle.  “Diversion” will surprise the dickens out of you.  Your world will expand while you sit there and let the magic enfold you.  Don’t worry – you won’t have to lift a finger for it to work.  This is theatre at its best.

Get thee thither.  N-O-W.

DIVERSION by Scott Organ, Directed by Seth Barrish,

WITH Tricia Alexandro, Thaïs Bass-Moore, Colleen Clinton, West Duchovny, DeAnna Lenhart, and Connor Wilson

Edward T.Morris (scenic design), Solomon Weisbard (lighting design), GinaRuiz (costume design), Geoff Grimwood (sound design) Samantha Tutasi (props)

Through December 21 at The Barrow Group, 520 Eighth Avenue.  Tickets HERE

By David Walters

If you’re a Laurie Metcalf fan, you’re gonna love this.

Little Bear Ridge Road, a Steppenwolf production now playing on Broadway at the Booth Theatre, is Laurie at her finest in a role that not many others would not be able to play with such percision. Her ability to combine such irascible charm, comic bitterness, and perfect timing in delivering her lines is unsurpassed.

It’s the beginning of COVID and far removed from Troy, Idaho, which is in itself far removed from any other settlement, Sarah (Laurie Metcalf) lives alone. She is a nurse and the medical establishment where she works has been bought by a conglomerate. Her hours are getting cut. Her nephew Ethan (Micah Stock) shows up as her brother, his methadone addicted father, has died and Ethan’s come to sell the house and get whatever money he can from anything that’s left from his father’s sad miserable life. Ethan is like Sarah in many ways as they are both angry emotionally lost lonely people fighting the world they inhabit. They are also the last two of a long line of Fernsbys that have been in Idaho for generations.

Over the next two years they end up living together and tormenting  each other (loving each other in their own way). Ethan makes a connection with James (Jon Drea), who becomes his boyfriend, and James brings some refreshing humanity to the two of them. James ends up pursuing his doctorate in Chicago, which of course, sends the delicate balance that was achieved into utter chaos. Ultimately all for the good of everyone.

Every actor, including Meighan Gerachis (as Vickie) in a very small role as a hospice nurse, was dynamite, filling out the distorted humanity of each of their characters. There are many comic moments in the butting heads of everyone, rants against the medical system here in the states, and thoughtful moments of connection between the characters as they suffer through their demons.

The set was “interesting” as it is a large triple recliner sofa on a turntable as the central focus, there’s a lot of television watching going on. The characters would slowly turn it to change place and time. I liked that aspect of it. The back wall of stone(?) though was questionable, especially when the characters were supposed to be outside.

I did have a bit of a problem with the script and that has led me to only give this an 82%. Exposition was blatant and clumsy, the final sentimental moment could be seen a mile away, but I will also say that overall there was a sense of reflection on the blight of living in this country, of modern American life, and the struggles of what it has become for so many.

But mainly, as I said, if you’re a Laurie Metcalf fan, you’re gonna love this.

——-

Little Bear Ridge Road written by Samuel D. Hunter and directed by Joe Mantello.

Starring: John Drea, Meighan Gerachis, Laurie Metcalf, and Micah Stock.

Scenic Design, Scott Pask; Costume design, Jessica Pabst; Lighting design, Heather Gilbert; Sound design, Mikhail Fiksel.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

The Surgeon and Her Daughters, by Chris Gabo, is an in-process African Blackwood carving that you can see the genius within about to pop out. It is at times poetical, compassionate, worldly, deep, universal, and truthful to a fault.

It’s 2016 and mom (Liza P. Fernandez) has retir It is at times poetical, compassionate, worldly, deep, universal, and truthful to a fault. ed from the military but is called back up for one more deployment. Before having to confront her two daughters (Yadira Guevara-Prip and Kana Seiki) with the news, she goes to a bar to try and deal with the reality of her situation. There she meets someone (Brian D. Coats) who she connects with on a deep spiritual level, who himself has lost a lot in his life and is thinking of ending it all. Their connection (“I like the way you frighten me.”) gives new life to the both of them.

Mom goes home and reveals all about her life to her daughters who are happy about the human connection, but immensely distraught at losing their mother for a period of time again and a hurtful fight ensues. Mom is deployed. Time passes and the gentleman who she connected with brings a rose bush over to plant while she is gone, introduces himself to the daughters, and while there, they find out that she has gone missing in country. The rest of the play deals with how the three of them handle and mishandle a loss that leaves nothing but un-fillable holes.

The play is itself bigger than its story which gives it a rich depth that caught many of the audience off-guard. It delves into the heart of performance art (a lovely speech about what performance is), capitalism and it’s cruelties, and the responsibilities we have to ourselves (“The system does not have to wake up and look in the mirror, I do.”) and others.

Tatiana Kahvegian’s spinning set is very versatile and together with Reza Behjat’s lighting, make good use of a restrictive playing space.

—–

The Surgeon and Her Daughters was written by Chris Gabo and directed by Adrienne Campbell-Holt, will run November 23-December 20 at Theater 154.

Colt Coeur theater company produced the show latching on to its urban setting and societal and political tensions that currently exist.

The cast: Brian D. Coats, Liza P. Fernandez, Yadira Guevara-Prip, Eden Marryshow, Johnny Sánchez, and Kana Seiki.

The design team includes Scenic Design by Tatiana Kahvegian, Costume Design by Sarita Fellows, Lighting Design by Reza Behjat, Sound Design by Salvador Zamora, and Props Design by Thomas Jenkeleit, with an original neo-soul score by Like Minds.

Theater 154 (154 Christopher St, New York, NY 10014) Tickets can be purchased HERE. $53-$104 Running time: 2 hours with a 10 minute intermission.

The play contains adult themes and strong language. Recommended for ages 13+.

title.rendered: A Christmas Carol at the Merchant’s House

content.rendered:
By David Walters

“Marley was dead: to begin with.”

From that first magnetic opening line you’ll be transported. Transported to another time and place that speaks directly to every time. There are some stories that one never grows tired of hearing and this is absolutely one of them.

A Christmas Carol, now performing at The Merchant’s House Museum (29 East 4th Street), is a pure delight from beginning to end. From the very beginning you’ll slip back in time, step by step, as you’ll enter the museum through the courtyard, into the garden, through the back door (due to reconstruction currently going on), and into the downstairs working portion of the house (kitchen and skullery). Up the stairs brings you into the warmly lit living room, decorated for Christmas in a Victorian way; you’ll take a seat directed toward a cleared space in front of the Christmas tree where Charles Dickens (Vince Gotton) performs all of the novella personifying every memorable character, their attitudes, and accents, with a sharp differentiation that brings them glowingly to life.

It’s a magical story, that I’m going to assume that everyone knows, made all the more magical being retold in this period space. The Merchant’s House Museum is the only New York City 19th century family home preserved both inside and out. That setting, and hearing Dicken’s words there, is transportive.

In 1867, Charles Dickens came to New York City for a month of sold out performances reading his beloved story A Christmas Carol in prose being A Ghost Story of Christmas. This production, presented by Summoners Ensemble Theatre, seeks to recreate that magical moment and time by spinning the clock backwards.

Please take this as a Currier and Ives Christmas card from me to you with the gift inside of urging you to go and ignite the spirit of Christmas within.

“I have endeavoured in this Ghostly little book, to raise the Ghost of an Idea, which shall not put my readers out of humour with themselves, with each other, with the season, or with me. May it haunt their houses pleasantly.” CD

A Christmas Carol at the Merchant’s House is haunting. Haunting in that you will remember the feeling of being a participant in this special moment throughout the holiday season.

”And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God bless us, every one!”

Go. You will be blessed.

——-

A Christmas Carol at the Merchant’s House, written by Charles Dickens, adapted by John Kevin Jones and Rhonda Dodd. Directed by Dr. Rhonda Dodd.

Performed alternately by Vince Gatton and John Kevin Jones now through December 28.

Tickets $50-$130. Click HERE to purchase tickets.

title.rendered: Scintillating Saint-Saëns: An InsideOut Revelation with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

In the luminous heart of Manhattan, the DiMenna Center for Classical Music once again proved why it has become a sanctuary for adventurous musical experiences. On this particular evening, the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony, under the visionary direction of David Bernard, unveiled Scintillating Saint-Saëns: The Full InsideOut Concerts® Experience, a program that stitched together history, virtuosity, and the irresistible charm of French Romanticism.

Maestro David Bernard describes the music with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony as they present Scintillating Saint-Saëns at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

Bernard’s trademark pre-concert talk, full of anecdotes that sparkle like chandeliers in a Parisian salon, set the evening aglow. Drawing on the orchestra’s storied legacy of innovation, community engagement, and deeply humanistic performance practice, he framed Saint-Saëns not as a museum relic but as a living, breathing spirit whose music still shimmers with immediacy. Bernard’s remarks, reflecting his own brand of raconteurship, reminded the audience how an orchestra’s essence lies not in abstraction but in storytelling — and how the InsideOut format, which seats listeners among the musicians, transforms the concert hall into an experiential agora.

Maxim Lando performs St. Saëns Piano Concerto No. 2 with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony as they present Scintillating Saint-Saëns at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

A charming moment occurred as pianist Maxim Lando greeted his former mentor, concert pianist Allison Lander, who had first known him at the Great Neck Music Conservatory when he was a bright-eyed three-year-old insisting on helping her carry music scores. Their reunion embodied the night’s theme: music as a lifelong, communal weave.

Camille Saint-Saëns by Eugène Pirou, 1880. Bibliothèque nationale de France, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Camille Saint-Saëns and the Architecture of Genius

A Composer of Chromatic Color and Contrapuntal Intellect

Saint-Saëns — that protean titan of French Romanticism — occupies a curious niche in music history. Though adored during his lifetime, his reputation was later overshadowed by Wagnerian thunder and Debussy’s diaphanous impressionism. Yet as Harold Schonberg reminds us in his seminal writings, Saint-Saëns possessed a “clarity of intellect clothed in sumptuous sonority” — a phrase that perfectly captures the two masterpieces featured tonight.

Brass and Woodwinds of the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony as they present Scintillating Saint-Saëns at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

Bernard’s program illuminated the composer’s intricate relationship with Franz Liszt, who famously championed him, and traced the evolving gravitas of the works as audiences worldwide continue to rediscover their architectural brilliance. In the spirit of Bernstein, Bernard invited listeners to appreciate how Saint-Saëns manipulates thematic transformation, harmonic rhetoric, and contrapuntal filigree with the mastery of a Renaissance craftsman and the technological daring of a 19th-century futurist.

Piano Concerto No. 2: Maxim Lando’s Brilliance in Motion

Andante Sostenuto: A Cathedral of Sound

The concert opened with Saint-Saëns’ Piano Concerto No. 2, a work whose improvisatory spirit and neoclassical wit draw from Bach, Beethoven, and the composer’s own organist alter ego. Lando’s opening cadenza unfurled like a Gothic arch — dramatic, spacious, and steeped in 19th-century chromaticism. His touch was assertive yet supple, creating the effect of an organ prelude reincarnated on the modern concert grand.

Maxim Lando, Pianist. Courtesy maximlando.com

As Bernard spun textures of diaphanous strings beneath him, Lando navigated each harmonic swerve with a rhetorical finesse reminiscent of the great French pianists — a fusion of clarity, steel, and aristocratic poise. The audience sensed instantly that we were in the company of greatness.

Second Movement: A Pearl of Perpetual Motion

The Allegro scherzando danced with crystalline lucidity. Lando’s articulation was mercurial, flecked with mercantile sparkle — the very definition of jeu perlé. Every figuration was sculpted with what one might call textured scintillation, creating an aural tapestry of elegance and precision.

French Horns and Woodwinds of the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony as they present Scintillating Saint-Saëns at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

Finale: Tarantella of Fire

The presto finale erupted with folkloric vigor, the rhythmic drive relentless, joyful, and feverish. Bernard shaped the orchestral response with his hallmark blend of athletic precision and emotional generosity. The Finale concluded in a jubilant conflagration, prompting an eruption of cheers.

Symphony No. 3 (“Organ”): A Cathedral Built of Light

Paolo Bordignon and the Majesty of Immersive Organ Sound

Saint-Saëns’ Third Symphony stands as a Showcase Symphony, a summation of his artistic life. With Paolo Bordignon at the digital pipe organ — voiced and spatially calibrated through a surround-sound system — the piece became a living organism of color and resonance.

Paolo Bordignon, Harpsichord and Organ. Courtesy paolobordignon.com

Bernard’s decision to incorporate a state-of-the-art digital instrument honored the composer’s entire sound world: majestic, mystical, and cosmologically immersive. Bordignon, celebrated organist and choir director of St. Bartholomew’s Church in New York City, infused each registration with French Romantic authenticity, from the ethereal whispers of the Adagio to the apocalyptic grandeur of the Finale.

Adagio – Allegro moderato

The first movement of the Symphony No. 3 emerged with the inevitability of tectonic motion—a vast architectural span in which Saint-Saëns seems to test the tensile strength of symphonic form. From the opening gesture, built upon the unmistakable Neapolitan tensions, David Bernard shaped the music with the deliberation of an artisan laying the foundation stones of a grand cathedral. The strings entered not as a mere section but as a collective breath, drawing listeners into a world where harmonic shadow and radiant light coexist in fragile equilibrium.

Bassoons, clarinets, and oboes with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony as they present Scintillating Saint-Saëns at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

As the movement unfolded, its contrapuntal layers intertwined with clarity, revealing voices often submerged beneath the surface. Bernard’s pacing allowed each structural arch to rise with organic purpose, while the orchestra’s deft handling of Saint-Saëns’s shifting textures suggested a rare fusion of emotion illuminated by intellect. In those moments when the music surged toward its first great climax, one felt a pulse of existence vibrating through the ensemble. It was a movement not merely performed but inhabited, a vast psychological landscape rendered with both precision and profound inner life.

David Bernard conducts the Saint-Saëns Piano Concerto No. 2, featuring Pianist Maxim Lando with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony as they present Scintillating Saint-Saëns at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

Adagio: A Meditation in Tonal Opalescence

The slow movement floated in an iridescent haze, strings and organ weaving a transcendent dialogue. Here, the InsideOut format achieved its purpose: listeners inside the orchestra felt the vibrations as if inside the body of a great cathedral. It was a moment of spiritual osmosis.

Scherzo: Virtuosic Alchemy

The scherzo’s contrapuntal labyrinths, punctuated by brilliance from pianists Maxim Lando and Keyi Wang, showcased Saint-Saëns’ genius for structural acuity. Bernard shaped the movement as a kaleidoscopic fugato, emphasizing the composer’s sophistication while never sacrificing kinetic sparkle.

Finale: A Triumph of the Human Spirit

The Maestoso burst forth with the organ’s radiant C-major proclamation. It was overwhelming in the best sense — seismic yet tender, monumental yet personal. As the orchestra surged toward its blazing apotheosis, one felt the entire hall transforming into a collective heartbeat.

Organist Paolo Bordignon performs in Saint-Saëns’ Symphony No. 3 with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony as they present Scintillating Saint-Saëns at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony: A Legacy of Excellence

With its storied history, innovative outreach, and associations with world-renowned guest artists, the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony continues to redefine what an orchestra can be. Bernard’s stewardship combines intellectual rigor with human warmth — a reminder that classical music, when presented with imagination, becomes a deeply communal, life-affirming force.

A Season of Musical Revelations Awaits

If this evening’s triumph serves as prologue, the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s 2025-26 season promises a series of musical revelations that will further cement the orchestra’s position as one of New York’s most vital cultural institutions. The season ahead unfolds like a carefully curated conversation between epochs and aesthetics, each concert offering its own unique dialogue with the musical canon.

Of particular note is the December 2025 concert, which promises to be a seasonal jewel in the orchestra’s crown. This program will undoubtedly weave together the festive spirit with the profound musical intelligence that Bernard and his ensemble bring to every performance. This musical celebration of Tchaikovsky’s The Nutcracker will surely transport audiences into that liminal space where time suspends and music speaks directly to the soul. Moreover, with the Family InsideOut Concerts® format continuing to dissolve boundaries between performer and listener, each concert becomes not merely an event to attend but a musical journey to inhabit—a chance to sit within the very heart of the orchestra and feel the music pulse through one’s being. For those who understand that great music-making requires not just excellence but also vision, not just technique but also soul, the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s upcoming season represents an essential pilgrimage, with December’s concert standing as a particularly luminous waystation on that journey toward musical enlightenment.

Maestro David David Bernard engaging with the audience at an InsideOut Concert with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Photo Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

excerpt.rendered: The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s radiant Saint-Saëns program at the DiMenna Center blended immersive magic, dazzling virtuosity, and profound emotional resonance. With David Bernard’s visionary leadership, Maxim Lando’s brilliance, and Paolo Bordignon’s majestic artistry, the evening ignited a passionate call to experience future PACS performances from within the very heart of the music.

title.rendered: Requiem and Revelation: A Transcendent Evening at St. Bartholomew’s

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

How curious it is that death should sing so beautifully. Last evening, enveloped in the Byzantine splendor of St. Bartholomew’s Church on Park Avenue, the American Symphony Orchestra and Bard Festival Chorale transformed mortality into transcendence through a program that enjoined the sacred with the sublime. Under the sagacious baton of Leon Botstein, this “Requiem and Revelation” concert unveiled treasures both familiar and forgotten, reminding us that the most fantastic art emerges from humanity’s most profound mysteries.

The Cornelius Revelation: An American Premiere

Indeed, Maestro Botstein has once again proven himself the musical champion of archaeology, exhuming Peter Cornelius‘s 1849 “Stabat Mater” from undeserved obscurity for its American premiere. Furthermore, this work proved a masterpiece of early Romantic sensibility, its rich chromatic harmonies weaving through the text like silk threads through a tapestry. Soprano Wendy Bryn Harmer soared magnificently through the work’s most demanding passages, her voice ascending with the effortlessness of incense through the nave’s soaring heights. Meanwhile, her three distinguished colleagues—mezzo-soprano Krysty Swann, tenor Eric Taylor, and bass Harold Wilson—each performing with remarkable aplomb, created a vocal constellation that illuminated Cornelius’s sophisticated choral architecture.

A view of Maestro Leon Botstein conducting Requiem and Revelation by the ASO at St. Bart’s in NYC. Photo by Matt Dine

Instrumental Excellence and Sacred Drama

Particularly noteworthy was the principal cellist’s contribution, whose instrument became the very voice of lamentation itself during the work’s most poignant moments. Subsequently, the strings embraced Cornelius’s intones with a warmth that suggested technical mastery bound to profound emotional intelligence. Brass, winds, and percussion, with an unexpected dramatic “gong” in the Cherubini work, were dramatic, solid, and sonorous. The a cappella segments, moreover, revealed the Bard Festival Chorale, under James Bagwell‘s direction, as an ensemble of exceptional refinement, with their voices blending with the architectural acoustics to create what Wagner might have termed a Gesamtkunstwerk—a total work of art.

L-R: Wendy Lynn Harmer, Soprano. Harold Wilson, Bass. Eric Taylor, Tenor, and Krysty Swann, Mezzo Soprano, performing in Requiem and Revelation by the ASO at St. Bart’s in NYC. Photo by Matt Dine

Cherubini’s Requiem: Death as Consolation

Following the intermission, Luigi Cherubini‘s 1816 “Requiem in C Minor” emerged as a study in contrasts. Where Cornelius had embraced Romantic expressivity, Cherubini offered Classical restraint transmuted into emotional profundity. Nevertheless, this work, too, revealed its own chromatic adventures, particularly in passages where the composer seemed to anticipate Berlioz‘s harmonic innovations. The orchestra’s strings displayed remarkable sensitivity to Cherubini’s nuanced voicings, while the brass proclaimed the Dies Irae with apocalyptic authority tempered by dignity.

Sacred or Secular: The Eternal Question

One cannot help but ponder whether these composers viewed their requiems as genuine acts of devotion or as concert works dressed in liturgical garments. Like Fauré‘s gentle Requiem or Mozart‘s incomplete Mass, these works seem to occupy that liminal space between cathedral and concert hall. Indeed, as T.S. Eliot observed in his “Four Quartets,” “prayer is more than an order of words, the conscious occupation of the praying mind.” Similarly, these musical orisons transcend their ostensible religious function to become meditations on the human condition itself.

Members of the Bard Festival Chorale at the ASO’s Requiem and Revelation by the ASO at St. Bart’s in NYC. Photo by Matt Dine

The Stokowski Legacy Lives On

How fitting that such revelations should unfold within St. Bartholomew’s, where the spirit of Leopold Stokowski—once the church’s organist and choir director—surely smiled upon the proceedings. This magnificent Byzantine-Romanesque edifice, with its perfect acoustical embrace, transformed each phrase into a three-dimensional immersive experience. Moreover, the space seemed to breathe with the music, its very stones resonating with centuries of sacred sound.

Masterful Musical Architecture

Botstein’s pre-concert talk and “A Note From the Director” in the program booklet had prepared the audience beautifully for the journey ahead. At the same time, Sonja Wermager‘s comprehensive program notes for tonight’s concert provided scholarly depth without sacrificing accessibility. Subsequently, this careful preparation allowed even newcomers to navigate the works’ complex emotional and spiritual terrains with confidence and context.

Requiem and Revelation by the ASO at St. Bart’s in NYC. Photo by Matt Dine

A Call to Musical Pilgrimage

As the final intones of Cherubini’s glorious denouement dissolved into St. Bartholomew’s hallowed silence, one could not escape the feeling that we had witnessed something precious—a musical colloquium in which the living and the dead conversed through the art of music and verse. Clearly, the American Symphony Orchestra continues to prove that adventurous programming and exceptional performance need not be mutually exclusive. Instead, they demonstrate that the most excellent service to “classical” music lies not in endless repetition of warhorses but in the courageous excavation of buried treasures, presented with the conviction and artistry they deserve.

Maestro Leon Botstein leads the ASO and Bard Festival Choral in Requiem and Revelation by the ASO at St. Bart’s in NYC. Photo by Matt Dine

title.rendered: What If They Ate the Baby?

content.rendered:
By David Walters

The dynamic creative team of Xhloe Rice and Natasha Roland hit another one out of the park in their presentation of What If They Ate the Baby? now performing until December 22 at Soho Playhouse.

It’s the 1950s in the U.S. with two central casting housewives visiting for the afternoon returning an empty borrowed casserole dish and catching up on their lives. There is the expected chit-chat about chores, husbands, and neighbors, but throughout it all there is an oppressive feeling in the air that all is not as it appears. And you’re right, it’s not.

There’s a knock at the door, and everything stops. There’s footsteps overhead, and everything stops. An off-handed remark and everything stops.

It’s apparent, that deeper inside, in the subtext of each character, things are flying at the speed of sound, seemingly without a rudder.

Highlighting this craziness is a soundtrack of 30 + songs, some from the period, but most much more current that stomp out the tempo of the production, keeping its convoluted trajectory on course.

The same dialogue repeats itself, but this time a little more off, a little more distorted. There’s an underbelly that seems to be getting scratched and gradually wakes from its slumber and begins to metaphorically spill everything out on the floor creating a world of absurdity that you could not have guessed it was heading.

“If you could eat one part of me what part would you eat first?” A hard decision at the best of times.

What Xhloe and Natasha do is artistically unique, brilliant, and distinct in the playing. They are absurdist clowns playing with physical theater that twists and turns from comedy, confusion, horror, absurdity, and darkly detailed dread, flipping back and forth from one second to the next. The precision in their movements both comment on and accentuate each moment. It’s a dance, it’s highly stylized choreography masterly performed that gives a multi-layered depth to their story.

The impetus of the show was, “inspired by 1950s McCarthyism and the overturning of Roe V. Wade in 2022.” This paranoia and fear of what is presented to the outside world, and the reality of what is playing underneath, behind closed doors, makes for a prime target for the genius of Natasha and Xhloe.

You can take a glimpse at their video HERE.

—–

Written, performed, and directed by Xhloe Rice and Natasha Roland.

Lighting design Angelo Sagnelli.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

At Soho Playhouse, 15 Van Dam Street, NYC, playing through December 22, all tix $45.50.

Run Time: 65 minutes

Age Recommendation: 13+ and strobe effects are utilized.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

A well-written play, as are all of Rajiv Joseph’s plays, makes it hard to create a bad show. His concentration is on relationships in difficult circumstances, and Gruesome Playground Injuries is another winner in that category.

Doug (Nicholas Braun) is accident-prone. So much so that his outside wounds become an identifying factor in who he is. The fact that he goes out of his way to put himself in situations that lead to his bodily harm, ignoring impracticalities and common sense, is also a part of who he is. He has an outlook on life as an innocent.

Kayleen (Kara Young) is accident-prone too, a train wreck with a heart. But not on the outside, on the inside. They both can’t help what they do to themselves and to each other, and despite their personal calamities, they remain a touch-point in each other’s lives.

The play jumps back and forth in time, beginning when they first meet in the nurse’s office at the age of 8, then fast-forwards to 23, then back to 13, forward again to 28, back to 18, jumping ahead to 33, back again to 23, and finally ending at 38. The non-linear storytelling keeps the audience engaged, putting the pieces of the puzzle of their lives together little by little. Both actors do a wonderful job in dancing between those moments of their characters’ lives. You can tell that they truly like each other, and it comes across in the playing.

Gruesome Playground Injuries is a warm, inviting play bereft of sentimentality and strong on relationship.  But for me, there’s always a little something missing in completing the stories that Rajiv tells. An incompleteness. Sort of like when finishing a puzzle you find that there is one piece, the last one, that is missing. There’s satisfaction in putting the 2999 pieces together, but the one tiny piece that has wandered off somewhere leaves you just a little less gratified. The ending of Gruesome Playground Injuries was that for me. After the deeply emotional pain, love, caring, and concern that we just went through, a metaphorical comment about a blue sky doesn’t seem quite enough.

That one missing piece is not enough to say don’t go (the other 2999 brought their own satisfaction). The relationship that Kara and Nicholas have created is charming and a delight to share in. Their playfulness reaches across the stage and touches the audience with deep humor and pathos.

—–

Gruesome Playground Injuries was written by Rajiv Joseph and directed by Neil Pepe.

Starring: Nicholas Braun and Kara Young.

Scene design by Arnulfo Maldonado; Costume design by Sarah Laux; Lighting design by Japhy Weideman; Sound design by David Van Tieghem.

Performing at the Lortel Theatre [121 Christopher Street]  until Sunday, December 28.

Run time: 90 Minutes
Contains mature content and language, recommended for ages 16 and older

Tickets can be purchased HERE – $42-$250

title.rendered: Triumphant Resurrection: MasterVoices Breathes New Life Into “Sweet Smell of Success”

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

In the grand tradition of theatrical rediscovery, Ted Sperling and MasterVoices have achieved something rather extraordinary with their semi-staged resurrection of “Sweet Smell of Success” at Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Frederick P. Rose Hall. What emerged on November 21-22 was not merely a concert reading but a full-blooded theatrical experience that, with devastating clarity, reminded us why Marvin Hamlisch considered this score equal to his Pulitzer Prize-winning “A Chorus Line.”

The cast and chorus of SWEET SMELL OF SUCCESS. Photo by Toby Tenenbaum

The production, under Sperling’s masterful baton, transformed what might have been a museum piece into a vivacious, breathing entity. One recalls Shaw’s observation that the theater exists to disturb the comfortable and comfort the disturbed—this “Sweet Smell” accomplishes both with serpentine grace. The narrative’s examination of power, corruption, and the price of ambition feels unnervingly contemporary, as if the ghost of Walter Winchell (upon whom J.J. Hunsecker is transparently based) still haunts our digital age of influencers and viral destruction.

The ensemble of SWEET SMELL OF SUCCESS. Photo by Toby Tenenbaum

Stellar Performances Illuminate the Darkness

Raúl Esparza, that chameleon of the American stage, embodies J.J. Hunsecker with a terrifying magnetism that would have made Alexander Mackendrick’s film incarnation proud. When he declares, “My column is the heartbeat of America,” one believes him utterly, even while recoiling from the malevolence beneath the charm. Esparza navigates the treacherous waters between paternal protectiveness and pathological control with the precision of a Swiss watchmaker.

Opposite him, Ali Louis Bourzgui as Sidney Falco delivers a performance of remarkable complexity. Fresh from his Theatre World Award-winning turn in “Tommy,” Bourzgui captures Sidney’s desperate scramble up the greasy pole of success with both comic timing and tragic depth. His rendition of “At the Fountain” becomes a hymn to American ambition, transforming from celebration to a cautionary tale before our eyes.

Brian Vaughn and Ali Louis Bourzgui in a scene from SWEET SMELL OF SUCCESS. Photo by Toby Tenenbaum

The revelation of the evening, however, was Lizzy McAlpine as Susan Hunsecker. Making her MasterVoices debut following her acclaimed Broadway bow in “Floyd Collins,” McAlpine brought a luminous vulnerability to Susan’s journey from gilded cage to hard-won freedom. Her crystalline voice in “Don’t Know Where You Leave Off” achieved that rare theatrical alchemy where song becomes pure emotion.

The Jazz Heartbeat of a Corrupted City

Noah J. Ricketts, as Dallas brought genuine jazz credibility to the role of the ill-fated musician, his crooning piano persona providing the production’s moral counterpoint to J.J.’s corrupt symphony. When Dallas sings “I Cannot Hear the City,” the Frederick P. Rose Hall seemed to hold its breath, the song becoming an oasis of genuine feeling in a desert of manipulation.

Aline Mayagoitia in a scene from SWEET SMELL OF SUCCESS. Photo by Toby Tenenbaum

Aline Mayagoitia invested Rita with a world-weary dignity that elevated what could have been a mere plot device into a fully realized woman surviving in a man’s brutal world. Her “Rita’s Tune” emerged as an unexpected highlight, a working-class aria that Shaw himself would have admired for its unsentimental portrayal of aspiration.

Hamlisch’s Score: A Rediscovered Jewel

The evening served as a powerful argument for Hamlisch’s own assessment of his work. The score, with Craig Carnelia’s razor-sharp lyrics and John Guare’s caustic book, creates a musical ecosystem that perfectly captures the fetid glamour of 1950s Manhattan. Songs like “Welcome to the Night” pulse with the syncopated rhythm of newsprint rolling off the presses. At the same time, “Dirt” becomes an anthem to American voyeurism that feels prophetically relevant to our social media age.

Raúl Esparza and cast in a scene from SWEET SMELL OF SUCCESS. Photo by Toby Tenenbaum

William David Brohn’s orchestrations deserve particular commendation, capturing both the jazz idiom and the theatrical grandeur without sacrificing either. Under Sperling’s direction, the MasterVoices Orchestra delivered these complex structures with precision and passion, reminding us why live orchestral sound remains irreplaceable in musical theater.

A Production That Transcends Its Format

Andrew Palermo’s choreography, working within the constraints of a semi-staged format, created moments of genuine theatrical magic. The nightclub sequences crackled with period authenticity while maintaining a contemporary edge. Alejandro Fajardo’s lighting design transformed the concert hall into a noir dreamscape, using shadow and spotlight to create the claustrophobic world of Times Square power brokers.

Lizzy McAlpine and cast in a scene from SWEET SMELL OF SUCCESS. Photo by Toby Tenenbaum

Tracy Christensen’s costumes deserved their own ovation, particularly Susan’s mink coat—a visual metaphor for her gilded imprisonment that becomes increasingly oppressive as the evening progresses. Ryan Howell’s scenic design accomplished miracles with minimal resources, creating distinct environments through suggestion rather than literal representation.

The Philosophical Resonance

What elevates this “Sweet Smell of Success” beyond mere entertainment, and it is commandingly entertaining, is its unflinching examination of American mythology. Like Arthur Miller’s great tragedies or Shaw’s own social comedies, it exposes the rot beneath the chrome, the human cost of what we call success. In our current era of influencer culture and viral destruction, J.J. Hunsecker’s ability to destroy lives with a few printed words feels less like period melodrama and more like a prescient warning.

Noah J. Ricketts in a scene from SWEET SMELL OF SUCCESS. Photo by Toby Tenenbaum

The production’s treatment of power—who wields it, who craves it, who is destroyed by it—recalls the great dramatic traditions from Sophocles to Shakespeare. When Susan finally turns the tables on her brother, using his own weapons against him, we witness not just personal liberation but a kind of democratic revolution in miniature.

A Triumph for MasterVoices

This production reminds one of MasterVoices’ unique position in New York’s cultural landscape. Under impresario Ted Sperling’s visionary leadership, they have become the premier organization for rescuing neglected masterworks from undeserved obscurity. Their ability to mount fully realized productions in concert format, maintaining both musical excellence and dramatic integrity, represents a vital service to American musical theater heritage.

Ali Louis Bourzgui and Raúl Esparza in a scene from SWEET SMELL OF SUCCESS. Photo by Toby Tenenbaum

Lizzy McAlpine and Raúl Esparza in a scene from SWEET SMELL OF SUCCESS. Photo by Toby Tenenbaum

excerpt.rendered: MasterVoices has given New York a gift with this “Sweet Smell of Success”—a production that argues forcefully for the work’s inclusion in the canon of great American musicals. For those seeking intelligent, adult musical theater that doesn’t sacrifice entertainment for enlightenment, this production provides a template for excellence. The ghost of Marvin Hamlisch surely smiles.

content.rendered:
By Brittany Crowell

Why do we tell stories?  Is it to foster empathy, forge understanding, build bridges between the aching chasms of the world around us?  Or perhaps to escape, to find ourselves, to discover qualities we never knew that we held?

In INITIATIVE, seven Millennials are growing up at the turn of the millennium; dealing with post-9/11 America & high school in small-town California.  Throughout Else Went’s five hour play, we watch them grow up – messily, falteringly, beautifully. 

The heart of this epic can be found in its characters, and in Went’s ability to make you fall in love with each and every one of them, troubled and flawed as they may be.  There’s Riley (Greg Cuellar), a dreamer and storyteller; valedictorian Clara (Olivia Rose Barresi), who takes on too much classwork and the weight of the world she’s inheriting; Lo (Carson Higgins), a troubled star athlete who is constantly finding measures of escape and refuses to look himself in the mirror; Em (Christopher Dylan White), a quiet youth who is afraid of his own desires; Kendall (Andrea Lopez Alvarez), a brassy and bright young artist, aiming to be desired; Tony (Jamie Sanders), an outsider to the group who finds himself on the other side of a fractured world; and Ty (Harrison Densmore), the big city transplant looking to find their place in the new school.

The ensemble cast feel like old friends, likely thanks to director Emma Rosa Went in addition to the long development process of the play and their involvement in it.  Not one minute of the five-hour performance feels tired, but each is filled with the vibrant and searching energy of youth and possibilities (fear and hope) for the future.  The audience is brought along for that journey – you laugh with them, you cry with them; all while you watch them misstep, learn, and grow into becoming.

Every single performance in the play is dynamic and strong, until you almost feel as though you’re a fellow classmate at the school and recognize yourself and your peers in them.  The Wents aim not to create nostalgia, but to breathe life into the past in order to heal and to build up a brighter future for us all – and I’d say that, leaving the theater at the end of the performance, I felt at once both transported and healed through their cathartic storytelling.

INITIATIVE is of a place and time specific to those growing up at the turn of Y2K and in post-9/11 America – where AIM becomes as much a tool for storytelling and character building as a d&d campaign, exquisite corpse, or high school essay assignment.  Mikiko Suzuki Macadams’ spatial design transports us into the halls of suburban America’s schools, Kindall Almond & Susan Hilferty’s costume design & dramaturgy (respectively) build our characters, Aisha Hamida (Props) and Chrisopher Akerlind (lights) take us between spaces, while S. Katy Tucker’s projection design overlays more magical worlds created by the teens as they escape into dungeons and dragons campaigns.

Asking again: why stories?  Well, they help us get through times of pain and uncertainty, allowing us to imagine a better world for ourselves, grow in the safety of fantasy into the humans that we wish we could be, test out identities with the hope of finding the bravery to bring the best of ourselves into the real world. Stories build community, provide safe spaces for growth and understanding, they fortify our souls.  

So, grab your twenty-sided dice and make a roll for initiative.  Who knows, hopefully you’ll hit a NAT20 and be the first to make it to the Public for this epic before is closes on December 7.

 

INITIATIVE – by Else Went; directed by Emma Rosa Went

FEATURING: Olivia Rose Barresi; Brandon Burk, Greg Cuellar, Harrison Densmore; Carson Higgins; Andrea Lopez Alvarez; Jamie Sanders; Christopher Dylan White; Marisa Brau-Reyes; & Jose Useche.

Scenic design by Mikiko Suzuki Macadams; costume design by Kindall Almond; costume dramaturgy by Susan Hilferty; lighting by Christopher Akerlind; sound by Angela Baughman; projections by S. Katy Tucker; props by Aisha Hamida; fight direction, Dan Renkin; Intimacy direction, Laura Hackman; dramaturgy, Sarah Lunnie; voice and text coaches, Julie Congress & Andrew Wade; stage management, Janelle Caso; line producer, Citali Pizarro; company management, Heather Fichthorn; production management , Aliyah Sall.  Produced by The Public Theater: Oskar Eustis, artistic director; Patrick Willingham, executive director (425 Lafayette St, New York, NY 10003).  Through Dec 7. www.publictheater.org/productions/season/2526/initiative

title.rendered: A Feast of Souls: “Pop Up Dinner Theater @Barlume Downstairs” by Suite524.org

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

There are theatrical evenings in New York that promise nourishment, and then there are evenings that feel like a communion of taste, emotion, and profound human recognition. “Pop Up Dinner Theater @Barlume Downstairs,” produced by Suite524.org, belongs firmly to the latter category.

Staged in the warm subterranean embrace of Barlume Downstairs, the event fuses four short plays with a four-course culinary progression, all threaded together by the whimsical, metaphysical wanderings of Frank — waiter, guide, philosopher — played by the ineffably charismatic Mateo d’Amato.

Mateo d’Amato and Amelia Gwaltney in a scene from “Fine Dining” in Pop Up Dinner Theater @VBarlume Downstairs. Photo by Delia Dumont

Frank does not simply serve drinks; he serves worlds. When he steps into view, blinking as if reacclimating to this century, he apologizes for being “a little scrambled eggs at the moment,” a confession made even funnier by the sincerity with which Domitrovich delivers it. As Frank recounts his curious past — apprenticing with an Anasazi flute maker, learning Maasai dances, falling in love across eras — he invites the audience to enter a space where time, flavor, and story mingle freely.

The structure, simple on paper, becomes thrilling in execution: each play arrives paired with its own course, and each course deepens the meaning of the play it accompanies. It is dinner as dramaturgy, theater as tasting menu. It’s also great fun!

Course I: Appetizers and Appetites — “The Cowboy”

The evening opens with a spread of blue crab toast, grilled halloumi, and a soppressata skewer, all accompanied by cocktails crafted at Barlume Downstairs. These flavors prepare the palate for the comedic combustion of The Cowboy, written by Michael D. Sharp and performed by a sharply tuned ensemble.

At a cocktail table of Manhattan financiers, Brian Reese transforms himself into the titular Cowboy, an unlikely philosophical catalyst in a conversation otherwise dominated by the sharp-tongued executives — the brilliantly incisive Drew Valins, the luminous Paulina Singer, the versatile Michaela Lind, and the effortlessly magnetic Nikki Valdez.

Brian Reese in a scene from “The Cowboy” in Pop Dinner Theater @Barlume Downstairs. Photo by Delia Dumont

As the bankers debate cattle markets, acquisitions, and a startlingly specific discourse on beef procurement and processing, the soppressata skewer becomes symbolic—an edible rendering of their tendency to pierce one another’s egos with corporate precision. The grilled halloumi, firm yet tender beneath its char, mirrors the Cowboy himself: warm-hearted, grounded, and entirely uninterested in the relentless striving that defines his tablemates. His monologue about Montana — the crisp air, the cedar-scented woods, the sacred quiet — settles over the audience like a fine mist. The blue crab toast, delicate yet intensely flavored, feels like the perfect culinary echo: a taste of something purer, softer, more vulnerable than the urban bravado surrounding it.

Course II: Spreads and Family Histories — “Peekos at Barlume”

The lights shift, wineglasses refill, and bowls of color arrive: fava bean hummus rich with earthiness, spinach tzatziki cool and refreshing, charred red pepper smoky and vibrant, walnut spread intricate and faintly bitter, and whipped ricotta soft as sighing clouds. These ingredients provide a sensory overture to Sandi Farkas’s poignant play Peekos at Barlume.

Here we meet Harriet, portrayed by the marvelous Sharon Ullrick, who sits armored in martinis and maternal mythologies. Across from her sits her son, Mitchell, played by Drew Valins in a performance beautifully distinct from his earlier one. Their conversation begins with the easy banter of a long-practiced habit but quickly plunges into grief, memory, and the fragile negotiations that define family.

The fava bean hummus becomes a grounding force, much like Harriet’s deep-rooted instincts to protect — and sometimes control — everyone around her. The whipped ricotta reflects Mitchell’s tenderness as he attempts to soften the blow of his news. The charred red pepper, with its smoky edge, mirrors Harriet’s volatility; its burn is the burn of a mother afraid to hear the truth. The walnut spread, layered with faint bitterness, speaks to the lingering sorrow they share. And the spinach tzatziki serves as the calming balm of humor, intermittently saving them from drowning in their own history.

Drew Valins and Sharon Ullrick in a scene from Peekos at Barlume in Pop Up Dinner Theater @Barlume Downstairs. Photo by Delia Dumont

When Mitchell reveals that his father, Harriet’s ex-husband, has died in a plane crash, Harriet’s anguished lament — sharp, holy, heartbreaking — slices through the room with an authenticity that leaves the audience breathless. It is a moment when food, memory, and story intertwine so naturally that one feels the emotional chords resonate across the table.

Course III: Main Courses and Emotional Indulgence — “Fine Dining”

As plates are cleared and anticipation rises, servers bring out the mains: chicken kebab, glistening and fragrant; calamarata, its pasta rings looping in tender spirals; and sirloin frites, indulgent and aromatic, rising from its plate like a culinary monument to pleasure.

This course pairs elegantly with Fine Dining, written by the formidable Eduardo Machado, a playwright whose command of emotional complexity is second to none. In this deliciously chaotic tale, Nikki Valdez, Chris Gray, Michaela Lind, Ellis Charles Hoffmeister, and Paulina Singer play a shifting constellation of ex-lovers who find themselves entangled in a dinner invitation from Paloma, whose glamor and emotional volatility rival the intensity of the sirloin frites before us.

The chicken kebab, with its sharp skewer threading tender pieces, becomes a metaphor for the characters’ emotional piercings — every confession and accusation passing from one to another like heat across a flame. The calamarata, with its spirals tangling into one another, mirrors the looping cycles of desire, jealousy, and self-delusion that define the group’s romantic history. And the sirloin frites, rich and unapologetically decadent, captures Paloma’s essence perfectly: bold, intoxicating, dramatic, and haunted by the fear that everything she treasures might one day slip away.

Machado’s writing balances sweetness with bitterness, creating a feast of humor, delight, and emotional flavors that feels perfectly paired with the course on the table.

Chicken Kabob and Steak Frites in “Main Course” at Barlume in Pop Up Dinner Theater @Barlume Downstairs. Photo by Delia Dumont

Course IV: Dessert and Delicate Truths — “See the Forest”

And then, dessert. A beautifully dusted tiramisu arrives — airy, layered, laced with rum and memory. Its name, meaning “pick me up,” becomes the poetic anchor of the final play, See the Forest, written by and featuring Michael Domitrovich.

Kelsey, played by the magnetic Amelia Gwaltney, opens with irrepressible joy as she recounts a night so wildly passionate she woke up “laughing — and slightly bruised.” Sarah Jordan Hupper, as Anya, responds with anxious restraint, creating a dynamic as layered as the dessert before us. Their dialogue flickers between candid yearning, emotional restlessness, and honest confession — moments as sweet and sharp as spoonfuls of mascarpone and espresso.

Enter Clark, played again with delightful crankiness by Eduardo Machado, who brings the kind of Shavian bluntness that slices through sentimentality. And soon after appears Chris, embodied with flirty brilliance by Ellis Charles Hoffmeister, whose swagger feels like the final dusting of cocoa atop the ensemble.

The tiramisu becomes a metaphor for the evening itself: the layering of emotions; the sweetness and bitterness of human connection; the pleasure of being lifted — even briefly — out of one’s everyday burdens.

Frank returns for one final meditation, reminding us that getting lost is often the only way to be found. His words settle gently into the palate, much like the lingering warmth of dessert.

Tiramisu at Barlume in “Dessert” at Pop Up Dinner Theater @VBarlume Downstairs. Photo by Edward Kliszus

A Theater of Appetite and Empathy

What Suite524.org accomplishes here is nothing less than a theatrical transformation. Dining becomes listening; listening becomes feeling; feeling becomes connection. This is theater that fills every appetite — sensory, emotional, intellectual — with extraordinary generosity.

It is the kind of experience William Archer would admire for its sincerity, and George Bernard Shaw for its wit and daring. More importantly, it is the kind of experience audiences will carry with them, tasting again in memory long after dessert has been served.

Suite524.org’s 2025–26 season promises more of this kind of theatrical communion — bold new works, immersive environments, and evenings that satisfy every craving for story, sensation, and connection.

A Feast of Souls: “Pop Up Dinner Theater @Barlume Downstairs” by Suite524.org

Presented by Suite524.org

Directed and written by Michael Domitrovich
Venue: Barlume Downstairs
325 W. Broadway, New York, NY 10013
info@barlumenyc.com • (212) 555-0199
Season & Tickets: Suite524.org

Run time is about 2 hours with no intermission.
Some adult language and themes.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

I’ve got the feeling that everyone who sees HardLove, now playing at SoHo Playhouse through December 12, will see a different play. They will see their play. That’s a magical thing because you can’t help but see yourself with all your accompanying baggage and viewpoints in what plays out between the characters in this two-hander.

Despite the bonfire of desire engulfing each character and the stated premise, “One night. No rules,” it’s an impossible setup. We can’t help but bring our expectations into any situation, especially one that is as cosmically charged as quick sex.

Meeting at a bar and both clothed and fueled by the two combustibles, desire and alcohol, ChiChi (Miray Beşli) and Theodore (Chandler Stephenson) tumble locked in an embrace into Theodore’s bedroom where they have disappointing sex (displayed in a wonderfully choreographed dance with each character facing the audience by Dougie Robbins). Disappointing because, despite the stated ground rule above, what’s good for the goose is not always good for the gander.

So, the stars didn’t align on that go around. Maybe try to mentally work out why it’s a disappointment and that will lead to putting the stamp of “Approved” on it. The thought come up that maybe they need practice at sex in order to have good sex. but really just need practice and connecting.

What the play also touches on, and is at the root of all the misses between ChiChi and Theodore, is how difficult it is to truly and meaningfully connect in a world where we experience so much of our learning, interactions, and emotions virtually. When we do get the opportunity to create a personal connection it’s not easy, it’s awkward, and sometimes feels impossible. We feel connected and seen online, but in person, there’s not the same feeling and there’s no screen to flip to for immediate gratification or escape if the now isn’t doing it for you.

On the other hand, is this all just a setup, a desperate attempt by a homeless narcissistic barfly to latch on to and manipulate a naive and trusting person to bleed him dry? And have we in the audience ourselves been fooled by ChiChi in the same way that Theodore has, wanting to believe and lured in by a sparkly power and energy that is only a firework display and not a warming hearth fire?

Now if all of that intellectual psychological explanation, exploration, and questioning has sparked your interest in HardLove, and piqued your curiosity about finding out more about yourself, then I suggest you’ll enjoy the play. If not, then there are plenty of other offerings in New York City. Just don’t do it online. Get out there and experience it live.

HardLove, Adapted by Esin İleri and Miray Beşli from the original Turkish play by Anıl Can Beydilli. Directed by Jee Duman, 

Starring Miray Beşli and Chandler Stephenson 

Choreographed by Dougie Robbins.

The show plays Thursdays and Fridays at 9PM at SoHo Playhouse, 15 Vandam St, New York, NY.

Tickets can be purchased HERE. All tix $34.50. Running time 60 minutes. Age restriction +14.

title.rendered: NOTHING LIKE BROADWAY at the Marjorie S. Deane Little Theater

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Nothing Like Broadway! presented at the historic Marjorie S. Deane Little Theater, is a buoyant tribute to the classic American musical. Writer-composer-lyricist David Rackoff constructs his show with the spirit of traditional craftsmanship: clear narrative purpose, honest emotional stakes, clever musical rhymes, and a belief that theater should engage both the intellect and affections.

L-R: Josey Miller, Marek Zurowski, Tyler Tanner, and Mychal Phillips in a scene from Nothing Like Broadway! Photo by Arden Dickson

The show’s approach embodies the kind of disciplined structure admired by William Archer—who championed clarity, sincerity, and dramatic coherence—while echoing the socially aware humor and artful provocations favored by George Bernard Shaw. Yet Rackoff’s work remains entirely its own: warm, mischievous, tuneful, and refreshingly earnest in an age saturated with irony.

A Historic Stage Reawakened

Nestled near Central Park West, the theater itself enhances the performance with its intimate charm and storied history. Once a haven for young artists, including Bob Hope and Tennessee Williams, the space carries the hum of past dreams—now rekindled through Rackoff and co-director Rosie Corr’s staging choices.

L-R: Joseph K. Ivan. Courtesy josephkivan.com and David Rackoff. Courtesy davidrackoffmusic.com

The actors frequently emerge from the aisles, appear from unexpected corners, and engage the audience as though the entire house were their playground. When Mychal Phillips begins Annabelle’s opening monologue from the first row before joining the stage, she immediately dissolves the barrier between viewer and performer. The result is immersive, lively, and playfully conspiratorial.

A Score Rich With Style and Theatrical Allusion

The musical textures crafted by Rackoff—and shaped by music director Joseph Ivan (who also plays Mr. Ivan in the show) — are both nostalgic and daring. A slightly worn spinet piano adds a wry, unstable shimmer to the harmonic landscape. Whether this sonic roughness was accidental or intentional, it lends an intriguing tension to the score, hinting at emotional fragility beneath comedic surfaces.

Marek Zurowski in a scene from Nothing Like Broadway! Photo by Arden Dickson

The music draws inspiration from operetta, early twentieth-century theatrical satire, and modern chamber-musical storytelling. Call-and-response patterns evoke Gilbert and Sullivan; rhythmic jaggedness conjures the theatrical angularity of early Stravinsky; sly harmonic shading recalls Weill.

Violinist/Violist Patrick Shelc, trumpeter Robert Williamson, with a drummer who contributed warmth, sparkle, and rhythmic vitality—a small ensemble producing a surprisingly expansive palette.

L-R: Marek Zurowski and Josey Miller in a scene from Nothing Like Broadway! Photo by Arden Dickson

The Cast: Four Performers, Limitless Charm

Marek Zurowski as Bixby

Marek Zurowski’s Bixby commands the evening with polished confidence and a lyric-dramatic tenor that fills the room effortlessly. He navigates the character’s duality—spy, storyteller, lover, and reluctant hero—with deft timing and a stylish wink. At times suave and at others delightfully baffled, Zurowski anchors the show with charisma and vocal heft.

L-R: Mychal Phillips. Courtesy mychalphillips.com and Marek Zurowski. Courtesy marekzurowski.com

Josey Miller as Kishka

As the faux-Russian spy Kishka, Josey Miller proves herself a comic whirlwind. Her firm accent, elastic expressions, and buoyant physicality are crowd-pleasing. She darts across the stage with controlled chaos, making each punchline land with spirited precision. Her number “You Only Love Me for My…” is a highlight of comic invention.

L-R: Mychal Phillips and Marek Zurowski in a scene from Nothing Like Broadway! Photo by Arden Dickson

Mychal Phillips as Annabelle

Phillips, whose character frequently instigates the plot’s twists, radiates charm. Her lilting soprano carries warmth and clarity, especially in “Nothing Like Broadway,” which reveals Annabelle’s blend of longing, theatrical bravado, and comic scheming. Phillips’ portrayal adds emotional ballast to the show’s more eccentric twists.

L-R: Tyler Tanner, Mychal Phillips, and Marek Zurkowski in a scene from Nothing Like Broadway! Photo by Arden Dickson

Tyler Tanner as Milo

Tyler Tanner brings sincere, beating-heart vulnerability to Milo—the stagehand yearning for artistic recognition. His ballad “If I Could Sing My Feelings” becomes one of the evening’s gentlest and most touching moments. Tanner’s shy earnestness provides a human counterweight to the espionage antics unfolding around him.

L-R: Josey Miller. Courtesy joseymariemiller.com and Tyler Tanner. Courtesy orlandoshakes.org

Plot, Antics, and a Touch of Apocalyptic Absurdity

The story unfolds with gleeful unpredictability: spies, double agents, secret formulas, daddy issues, theatrical dreams, and an unexpectedly looming nuclear threat tied to Annabelle’s father’s corporation, “Squeedle.” Rackoff and Corr embrace farce, sincerity, and comic subversion, choreographing action that bursts into aisles and climbs into musical flights of imagination. The narrative twists remain clear despite their complexity—a nod to the dramaturgical rigor Archer often praised.

By the finale, the characters’ antics give way to a surprisingly heartfelt affirmation: that art, authenticity, and vulnerability are enough to save both our inner worlds and, perhaps, the outer one as well.

NOTHING LIKE BROADWAY! Courtesy nothinglikebroadway.com

THEATER INFORMATION & TICKETS

Show Tickets and Information

Marjorie S. Deane Little Theater
West Side YMCA
5 West 63rd Street
New York, NY 10023
Box Office: 212-912-2600

Runtime 2 hours and 10 minutes, including intermission

excerpt.rendered: “Nothing Like Broadway” celebrates imagination, heart, and theatrical playfulness. With its spirited cast, clever score, and intimate staging, it rekindles everything audiences adore about the musical form. A fresh, funny, hopeful evening that leaves you eager for the Marjorie S. Deane Little Theater’s vibrant season ahead.

content.rendered:
By Victoria L. Dammer

Las Vegas. The worst place to live if you have a gambling problem. And if you have dementia, well, it doesn’t make a hill of beans where you live.

So begins the comic-drama world premiere of The Drop Off, written by award-winning playwright James Anthony Tyler and directed by Delicia Turner Sonnenberg. Allain (Chantal Jean-Pierre) is the gambling-addicted daughter of Delphina (Joyce Sylvester), a seasoned citizen lost in another world of her own at Deer Lakes Assisted Living in Vegas.

Allain has no choice but to put her mother in assisted living; she’s gambled away her home, her relationship with her son, and caring for her mom is no longer an option. Allain has lost her soul, her money, and her ability to tell right from wrong. That’s addiction.

In her new home, Delphina’s dementia agitates her, and she wants to go back to Allain’s home. “I am not staying here,” Delphina proclaims. She’s scared, confused, and defiant. Allain is far from sharing the details of her messed-up life. Delphina wouldn’t understand what had happened to her daughter anyway. Dementia is a sad, life-crippling disease for both the patient and the family.

Allain has trouble coping with her mother’s illness, enhanced by her own anxieties, and Jean-Pierre gives a stunning performance as a woman out on a ledge. Mimi (Harmony Harris), Delphina’s warmhearted caretaker, works hard to calm both mother and daughter as they transition to Deer Lakes. Delphina adjusts; Allain needs more than a loving caretaker to change her life.

Sylvester delivers her lines like a natural comedian, and the audience immediately endears to her. She is befriended by a resident named Crystal (Niambi), who repeats the same stories. Much to Delphina’s delight, Crystal is the friend who will make her transition to living in a senior citizen’s home that much easier.

The Drop Off is a story of transition and addiction, with a compassionate look at the devastating effects of dementia, albeit with a comical side of humanity. The Drop Off offers a glimpse of what so many families may face with elderly parents.

The Drop Off at New Jersey Repertory Company through November 23rd. Written by James Anthony Tyler and directed by Delicia Turner Sonnenberg. Starring Harmony Harris, Chantal Jean-Pierre, Joyce Sylvester, and Niambi. Scenic design by Jessica Parks; costume design by Nicole Jescinth Smith; lighting design by Jill Nagel; sound design by Nick Simone; stage management by Kristin Pfeifer; production assistant Ian Duhart.

 

THROUGH NOVE 23 – New Jersey Rep
