content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

What do you give a woman who has started out with less than nothing, married a gazillionaire, lost everything, got it all back and then lost her family AND had a documentary film based on all of the above?  You give her a musical. And give her a star.

The Queen of Versailles is the musical, Kristen Chenoweth is the star and Jackie Siegel is the real life person who is still out there super-sizing everything she can get her hands on.  And F. Murray Abraham is the real life David Siegel who invented time share vacations and found an unending supply of suckers to gobble them up.

Kristen Chenoweth; Photo by Julieta Cervantes

First the good part – there is a boatload of talent on that stage, starting with Chenoweth herself whose voice and energy are elevated and on display the entire time.  Pablo David Laucerica as Louis XIV and Cassondra James as his unfortunate bride Marie Antoinette are startling.  They make the music of clever angels seem like the easiest thing in the world and come close to revealing that this production is an opera of its own.  Melody Butiu as Sofia rips our hearts out singing of her family who she has not seen in 18 years because she was raising the Siegel children.  And two of those children Victoria (Nina White) and Jonquil (Tatum Grace Hopkins) are running a close second to Chenoweth and picking up the torch as we watch.  Even Abraham can sing – who knew?  The talented “chorus” are the ones running the whole shebang.  They move furniture, run video equipment, wear hard hats and climb to the far reaches of the set, all the while singing in glorious harmonies.

Kristin Chenoweth and Cassondra James; Photo by Julieta Cervantes

A special nod to the scenic design by Dane Laffrey and costume design by Christian Cowan that take us from the time of Louis XIV to the present day vulgarity of the Siegel Versailles – More gold than the Lincoln Bathroom…. The costumes of Louis court are off the charts.  And WHERE were they storing the Siegel Versalles before it appears onstage???

So talent – check.  Discipline and skill – check.  Visuals – check.

On the other hand, if you are looking for a a story line that engages and excites you, well, that is not happening here.  First of all this story is all about excess and greed, of which there is plenty, but there isn’t a redeeming quality to be seen anywhere. Not even in a farce kind of way. Hence, there is no one to root for, and without a someone to root for, there is no story.  The tale, such as it is, is as flimsy as tissue paper and falls apart under the slightest scrutiny.  Ditto for the music that does not further said tale, but is more of a weigh station.  With the conclusion of each number we are no further along than we were before.

So, despite the enormous effort, and the tons of talent and work that went into making this production happen, we leave uninspired and embarrassed that this story, such as it is, was elevate and put on a stage.  For some of us the theatre is our temple.  To see it treated so poorly is a mystery.

A damn mystery.

QUEEN OV VERSAILLES – Book By Lindsey Ferrentino, Music by Stephen Schwartz, Director Michael Arden

Music direction by Mary-Mitchell Campbell, choreography by Lauren Yalango-Grant and Christopher Cree Grant, and direction by Tony Award winner Michael Arden., scenic & video design by Dane Laffrey, costume design by Christian Cowan, lighting design by Natasha Katz, sound design by Peter Hylenski, hair & wig design by Cookie Jordan, orchestrations by John Clancy,

Kirsten Chenoweth, F. Murray Abraham, Melody Butiu, Stephen DeRosa, Greg Hildreth, Tatum Grace Hopkins, Isabel Keating, Nina White. Yeman Brown, David Aron Damane, Drew Elhamalawy, Christopher Gurr, KJ Hippensteel, Cassondra James, Andrew Kober, Jesse Kovarsky, Pablo David Laucerica, Travis Murad Leland, Ryah Nixon, Shea Renne, Michael McCorry Rose, Grace Slear, Anne Fraser Thomas, Jake Bentley Young

At the St. James Theatre.  Tickets HERE.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Margret Echeverria

Archduke, written by Rajiv Joseph, directed by Darko Tresnjak now playing Off-Broadway at Laura Pels Theatre examines the seeds of the first World War.  You know, that war our high school history teacher glossed over in a rush to cover WWII before the mid-year exam, so that we could really dive into the Korea and Vietnam conflicts by Spring.  Hello, dark humor.  This production reveals the absurdity of our un-evolved species continuing to lather rinse and repeat the cycle of war.

In 1914 Belgrade, there was an abundance of poor and sickly boys thanks to tuberculosis and deep economic class disparity.  Two such nineteen year old boys, Gavrilo (Jake Berne) and Nedeljko (Jason Sanchez), meet at midnight in a warehouse where they were sent to wait for an

ARCHDUKE with Jason Sanchez, Jake Berne and Adrien Rolet. Photo by Joan Marcus

opportunity.  A scene unfolds revealing their innocence and pliability mixed with existential fear.  Berne and Sanchez meet the dramatic challenge with grace as they raise a mirror gently to our humanity and we grin into the reflection of our painful dilemma.  The human condition is to hunger for nourishment and love, but men are taught to strive most of all for purpose.  Eventually these two are joined by a third young man, Trifko (Adrien Rolet) who, after a series of misunderstandings and bittersweet revelations about imagined salvation in women and sandwiches, escorts them to their destiny.

The three youthful recruits sit at the table of master manipulator, Dragutin “Apis” Dimitrijevic (Patrick Page).  Page brings bright engaging charisma to this historical figure.  His comedy is in his adroit physicality as well as in his palpable love for Joseph’s turns of phrase.  The language sparkles as Page speaks in his commanding signature voice like a preacher over the three boys, pushing them on board the train to Sarajevo to commit acts of treason. He seduces them with exaggerated stories of his own heroism over a table of endless good food, making grand predictions of the boys’ exaltation in martyrdom to liberate their oppressed bretheren.

The formula is familiar:  The minds of young idealists are lathered into a frenzy of righteousness up against those who are different yet live among us.  The manipulated – often kids – rinsed of their guilty failures, usually economic, are made beautiful in gloves and boots shiny with empty promises.  Then the terrible destruction, backed by those inebriated with greed, is easily repeated once again as it has been wrought upon the world since the beginning of time.

Behind the power of Dimitrijevic is his “lady cook,” Sladjana (Kristine Nielsen), possibly the only fictional character in the piece, but entirely necessary.  Nielsen is a character actress as delicious as the victualing she lays on Dimitrijevic’s table.  Her skillful balance of mirth and truth are breathtaking as she deftly pulls back the curtain on the misogyny deep in the murky roots of any nationalist movement.  Nielsen’s non-verbal expressions are welcome comic relief indeed, yet a scene between her and Berne while surrounded by heavy Christian iconography gave me chills as the two revealed what actually speaks to their souls.  These men who choose violence are running away from feminine wisdom that they are told is wicked witchcraft and the women in these hellscapes are hiding their true magic under cloaks of darkness in the name of survival.

Without the shock and awe of mid-century technology used for inexplicable evil and dictators so horrible they become mythical super villains, the narrative of the first World War feels less impossible than that of the second.  Perhaps that tangibility is why we don’t talk about it as much.  Archduke illustrates the gritty genesis of man-made disaster and we laugh when we see ourselves as we are right now — so vulnerable to mass hysteria.  Yet this piece, through allowing us a little chuckle at the gallows of history, gives us a glimpse of hope for our future.

ARCHDUKE by Rajiv Joseph, directed by Darko Tresnjak

WITH Jake Berne (Gavrilo), Kristine Nielsen (Sladjana), Patrick Page (Dragutin “Apis” Dimitrijevic), Adrien Rolet (Trifko), Jason Sanchez (Nedeljko)

Set Design, Alexander Dodge; Costume Design Linda Cho; Lighting Design, Matthew Richards; Sound Design, Jane Shaw; Hair, Wig & Makeup Design Tom Watson; Fight Direction, Rocío Mendez; Production Stage Manager, Katie Young.
Through December 21 Harold and Miriam Steinberg Center for Theatre Laura Pels Theatre111 West 46th Street, New York, NY.  Get tickets here.  Running time: 2 hours, including a 15-minute intermission.

@graph.description: In the summer of 1978, while watching a performance of A Murder is Announced on the London stage, Margret fell in love with the theatre. Born and raised in Cedar Falls, Iowa, Margret came to New York City in 1994. She was admitted to Newmyn’s Nose Limitless Theatre Limited, an innovative and award winning improvisational company, in the summer of 1995 and eventually became a member of the company’s board. Margret starred in the critically acclaimed short film Jigsaw Venus by Dean Capsalis in 2000 (Best Actress, Buenos Aires International Independent Film Festival) and her film career was begun. She played the adorable Fag Hag (GenX does not find this term offensive at all), Audrey, in both A Four Letter Word (2007) as well as Violet Tendencies (2010), films by Casper Andreas and Jesse Archer. She has a co-starring role in Max Emerson's film, Hooked. Always sentimental about performing for a live audience, Margret penned and performed Orangerie, a one-woman show exploring the subject of finding love while traveling non-traditional avenues, which premiered at the Bowery Poetry Club in November of 2005 and ran through the spring of 2006 to critical acclaim. After Margret’s family survived the death of their son, Gavin, to SIDS in 2011, she penned her last one woman show, Finding Gavin, which premiered in New York City in 2015. She was on the season finale of Law & Order SVU in 2021. Margret studied Acting at Regent’s College in London, Classical Voice and Opera at the Royal Academy of Music in London, and Acting at Sally Johnson Studio here in New York City. She has a BFA in Acting from Rockford University. Margret is also a published poet. She lives in Yonkers, NY with her daughter, Alyson.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

The Story of The Baker’s Wife at Classic Stage Company:  A long time ago – a long, long time ago – kind of around the same time that Brigadoon made its once-in-a-century appearance except not quite – that kind of a time – there was a little village located in Nowhere France by the name of Concorde.  This was s town where there were no secrets even if you wanted to have a few.  More important than that, however, is the fact that when we are ushered into the town’s story it is because Concorde has been without a baker for SIX WEEKS.

Mon Dieu.

We witness some discussion about the thoughtlessness of the old, now deceased, baker that fills the time while the townsfolk are filling the well of anxiety that being bread-less produces.  Bread is, after all, the staff of life.  The aroma fills the soul and the physical reassurance that all is well.  As backdrop to this hubbub we are serenaded by our guide Denise (Judy Kuhn) whose sings to us with simplicity and majesty.  Her position as guide has a little Anatefka in it.  The story is there because WE are there.  The two cannot exist without the other.  Rest assured, she tells us, life is made up of small moments, and it only takes one to change you forever.  Kuhn is exquisite, and we are drawn into her web within the first few notes.

The fable is set, and the Baker, Aimable Castagnet (Scott Bakula) who is, as his name suggests, a kind and generous man, arrives with his w-i-f-e Geneviève Castagnet (Ariana DeBose).  Genevieve is not so kind and generous.  Not that she is mean. No, no.

She is restless.

She is decades younger than Aimable and for reasons unexplained, she is feeling out of sorts.  So straightforward is the text and the lyrics that we don’t care much for the whys and wherefores.  We watch this enchanted collection of lives play out without a question.

When  a young handsome man, Dominique, (Kevin William Paul) falls in love with Genevieve at first glance, his passion and impetuous nature sweep her off her feet, out the door and out of town.

The result is that the Baker is worse off than when he arrived.  Bereft, forlorn and shattered.  The man who is not a drinker goes on an epic bender.  There is no point to anything.

And bread?  Forget about it.

This calamity puts the townsfolk into a tizzy.  I mean, sure, they like the Baker and his wife, but more important than friendship is the bread, the bread, the bread.  They must remedy the situation.  Find Genevieve and bring  her back to the Baker.  Even if they have to cooperate with one another.  Old grudges. and there are so many than no one remember where they started,  must be sidestepped.  Broken hearts mended.  Risks taken.  This bread business is a matter of life and death.

The Baker’s Wife ia a parable: have faith that it WILL work out.  What makes this production exceptional is the glorious work of the cast whose voices must reach the planets from which other beings watch us.   DeBose opens her mouth and sings in the colors of the rainbow.  Scott Bakula is a surprise gift.  His vocal approach to the baker’s sweetness and inevitable slide into despair is robust and tender all in one.  Bakula and Debose wear their hearts of their sleeves.  Without our noticing they hand those hearts to us for safe keeping.  It is not until the conclusion of the show that we realize our part in the tale and hand this precious cargo back.

And their chemistry?  Fuhgeddaboudit.  Off the charts.

Everything grand can and should be said about the entire ensemble.  Under the direction of Gordon Greenberg they trust each other like runners in a relay.  They hand the story off to one another and lead us deep into the hearts of this town.  Their voices. punctuate with precision and convince us we are hearing angels sing.

No surprise story-wise – everything does work out.  Not in a syrupy 1950’s musical way.  This production gives us a resolution that is as simple and profound as life’s magic pageantry.  No pronouncements.  No protestations.  Just two people who have infected a village with their quest for a happy loving life.

And that, as the song goes, changes everything.

AND THEN ONE DAY, SUDDENLY, SOMETHING CAN HAPPEN,

IT MAY BE QUITE SIMPLE, IT MAY BE QUITE SMALL

I don’t care how heart-hardened you are – this one is a show for your jewel box..

PS : You can find a fascinating history of the CSC’s incarnation and history of this production HERE

 

THE BAKER’s WIFE – Book By Joseph Stein, Music & Lyrics By Stephen Schwartz, Choreography By Stephanie Klemons, Directed By Gordon Greenberg, Based On The Film La Femme Du Boulanger, By Marcel Pagnol, Jean Giono, Adapted From “Jean Le Bleu” By Jean Giono

WITH Scott Bakula,  Wendi Bergamini, Savannah Lee Birdsong, Arnie Burton, Robert Cuccioli, Alma Cuervo, Ariana Debose, Kevin Del Aguila, Bill English, Zachary Freier-Harrison, Samantha Gershman, Nathan Lee Graham, Judy Kuhn, Sally Murphy, Manu Narayan, Mason Olshavsky, Kevin William Paul,  Will Roland, Hailey Thomas

Charlie Alterman(Music Direction), Jason Sherwood (Set Design), Catherine Zuber (Costume Design), Bradley King (Lighting Design), Jason Crystal (Sound Design)

At Classic Stage Company  – 36 East 13th Street, New York, NY 10003, 212.677.4210

Through December 21.  TICKETS HERE

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

The Popes of Farragut Street, written & directed by Melanie Maria Goodreaux and having its premiere run at Theater for the New City, is a high-spirited dive into faith and love. Set in an auto shop in New Orleans’ 7th ward it is the story of the owner, Conrad Patsy (Benjamin Rowe), and his group of mechanics Ducky (Marco Cunha), Pee Wee (Javan Robinson), and Shade (Aristotle Stamat), their life in the shop and outside of it.

They are all excited and nervous for two reasons. One, there is a hurricane heading straight for New Orleans, AND Pope Leo XIV is in town! They are celebrating the Pope’s visit because he is the first Pope to have creole blood running through his veins. It is also the story of Conrad’s wife, Rachel Patsy (Hollie Harper), who has been married to Conrad for years but he in truth only loved her for exactly three days. Conrad has decided to reignite the love he truly had for one woman Mable Preston (Christian Neal). Now the time has come for both Conrad and Rachel to try to capture love in their life.

Day three of their short love affair Rachel was pregnant and their nonbinary child Lester (Zus Santos) is grown and working for dad. Lester is trying to make his way through the maze of his father’s love for him and the hate he feels for his mother. He is trying to find his way in a world where love was a confusing part of his identity. And it is all happening with knee- slapping humor.

Throw in two more of these  characters, the local hierarchy of Catholicism, Father Omar (Derick Storme), who has lost his faith to the throes of passion for a woman, and the self-titled Pope of Farragut Street, Pope Violet (Vienna Carroll) who doles out words of wisdom reminding them all about another kind of love, the love of God and you have a wonderful congestion of highly motored individuals all looking for conection.

Pope Violet tells them all, “Cut a hole in the roof with your hatchet and wait for God to see you.” A metaphor for their lives. Make a move to be seen and you will find your place.

In this exciting production every character is standing on the edge of a cliff, itching and ready to jump off into a new realm, struggling within themselves and with one another to get what they want. In the end, all will make a move!

The Popes of Farragut Street is beautifully written and directed with speed and hilarious, sometimes outrageous, humor. Goodreaux has created a Shakespearean dramedy that will make you happy you are there watching these stunning actors tear the stage up!

Set designers Lytza Colon and Gregory Paul have made a magical labyrinth of auto shop and places of worship, all of it as if we the audience climbed down into a cave in the center of the world and are watching this story unfold.

The Popes of Farragut Street is a marvelous biting theatrical production with creative honest performances that meld to make a great night at the theater.

The Popes of Farragut Street written and directed by Melanie Maria Goodreaux

With: Benjamin Rowe , Hollie Harper, Zus Santos, Christian Neal (Mable Preston), Derick Storme (Father Omar), Aristotle Stamat (Shade / Tucker), Marco Antonio Cunha (Ducky), Javán Robinson (Pee Wee), and Vienna Carroll (Pope Violet).

Creative team features prop and set designers Lytza Colon and Gregory Paul; sound/visual designers Luke Santy, URB ALT/Boston Fielder, and Anthony Harper; lighting designer Alexander Bartenieff; costume/wardrobe director Billy Little; movement/choreographer Kristina King; casting director Linda Greene; and graphic designers Tim Fielder and Diane Sullivan. Stage managers are Christopher Bello and Taylor Bertman. Producers include  Mark Holloway, David Kahl, Norah Lawlor, Anthony Harper, and Bruce Morrow.  The executive producer is Crystal Field, Executive Director of Theater for the New City.

Running Time: 2 hours with one ten minute intermission

Tickets HERE
The show is wheelchair accessible.

Theater For The New City 155 1st Avenue
(between 9th and 10th Street)
New York, NY 10003

content.rendered:
By David Walters

If you’ve ever been part of a family and now have stepped away, Harvest by Jason Pyette, will bring you right back there. Though set in wheat country in Montana, family is family everywhere and the dynamics of one family play out in all others, worldwide, throughout time.

Montana Actors’ Theatre has brought this production to New York (a New York premier for everyone involved), now performing at Chain Theatre only through November 22.

Everything about this production is Montana, the set, the actors, the play, the story. The audience is transported from the very beginning just looking at the set prior to the house lights going down as the set is so authentic it too seems to be a character in the play. It’s the living/dining room of a Montana farmhouse that looks like it was cut out, put on a truck, and plunked down in the theatre. That house has been lived in.

Why I’m going on about the set is that the actors truly treat it like the home that they were raised in. That comfortableness adds to the reality and viability of this show. It’s not a perfect show, some moments could be cut, the acting has highs and lows, but none of that matters as the story of Harvest and what it’s saying brings in the audience emotionally and gets them invested in each of the characters. It wasn’t just me either; audience members from Australia and Italy that were sitting with me (who also had families so we ended up discussing our experience of the show afterwards) felt the same emotional draw to what happened on stage. It’s universal.

The patriarch of the family had a heart attack a year ago, and though he’s capable of it, hasn’t really gotten out of bed since. Of the six kids (now adults, five boys and one girl), only one, John (Chad Zuelkehas), stayed on the farm to try and keep it going. The daughter (Tylyn Turner), through some slight trickery, has managed to get everyone to return to the farm to try and convince them to stay a week and help with getting the wheat in on the 160 acre farm. Through much cajoling and guilting, they all say yes. Weather, fire, ancient equipment that keeps breaking, and the animosity of personal histories that have led them as adults to not really like each other that much conspire to keep them from their goal. As with many families, they never let each other grow up. The fabric of this family has been rendered and this in turn is reflected in the farming community around them that no longer operates the way it used to.

I’ve seen Broadway family dramas that didn’t have the emotional depth and punch that Harvest has. Well worth a look.

—–

The Harvest written and directed by Jason Pyette.

The cast features Pam Veis, TC Knutson, Grant Olson, Brian Gregoire, Tylyn Turner, Chad Zuelke, Aylan Pratt, and Samantha Pollington.

Lighting design by Brian Easton, sound design by Evan Leeds, original music by Matt Springer, and costume design by Angela Riggin.

November 6–22 at Chain Theatre.

Tickets can be purchased HERE. All seats $20.

content.rendered:
By Yuval Jonas

The poet and critic Mark Van Doren wrote that “The subject of “Richard II” is the reign and deposition of an English king. It is also the beauty of the English language considered an instrument upon which music can be made.” One of Shakespeare’s few plays with no prose whatsoever, Richard II is indeed all poetry. The plot is thin. There is neither a hero nor so much of a villain, rather a victim of self-indulgence. Yet the poetry is extraordinarily beautiful. Shakespeare endows Richard with lyrical musings reminiscent of his most powerful creation yet to come: Hamlet.

In a play that depends so heavily on its main character—where most others lack, to borrow a term from Harold Bloom, “inwardness,” except for John of Gaunt, who dies early—Michael Urie, as the incompetent king, delivers powerfully. In this production from Red Bull Theater, directed and adapted by Craig Baldwin, Urie controls the language. He performs the speeches almost to perfection; he is dynamic with rhythm and pitch, full of meaning, and perhaps most important of all, he recognizes the irony—Shakespeare’s favorite ingredient.

Baldwin frames the production as a memory play. Richard roams in a glass-box prison cell as the audience enters. The show begins with his final speech, then circles back through the events leading to his downfall. Like Tom in The Glass Menagerie, he remains on stage throughout, observing. This concept makes some sense: again, as Bloom says, “Richard’s imagination is trapped solipsistically in the prison of his petulant self.” But Baldwin repeatedly inserts himself as director rather than letting the verse do its work. Indeed, the great tension in this production is the beautiful performance that Urie gives us, and the overpowering presence of Baldwin’s direction and the production.

The 1980s costumes are too much. The music is too much. The trial by battle in the first act is an MC-led event with Russian roulette revolvers. Much of the acting leans on over-gesturing and over-stressing the verse. The exceptions are Urie and James Seol as Green; Seol lets the words flow naturally and urgently, giving his heart to the performance.

This is the great sin of modern theater: the director as king. With the (relatively) recent invention of film, such dominance makes sense. But in the ancient form of theater, the words and the performers should reign.

The ending is where the production sharply departs from the play. Shakespeare gives Richard an inglorious death—he is attacked by strangers, dying without dignity, swept off to nothingness. Baldwin instead creates a Hollywood betrayal: Aumerle (Richard’s cousin, close confidant, and in this production, lover), played by David Mattar Merten, shares a long kiss with Richard before stabbing him. Merten’s lines were originally spoken by a simple groom, almost a stranger to Richard. The production conflates Aumerle with the groom, servants, and Exton, turning the scene from something dirty, devoid of any nobility, into romance and melodrama, missing Shakespeare’s point.

Shakespeare’s genius in this play, and others, lies in how little the king’s death matters. As Richard says, “And my large kingdom for a little grave, / A little, little grave, an obscure grave.” Like in Hamlet, Shakespeare doesn’t end with one of the most beautiful lines in all of literature (as others would have done)—“And the rest is silence”—but with Fortinbras taking over. The “hero” is simply swept away. Baldwin instead makes it mean something, makes it cinematic, when the whole point is how empty it is.

What remains, despite all this, is Urie’s remarkable performance. He gives us the Richard who performs his own tragedy, who knows the crown is both everything and nothing. More of the verse and less of the production’s flashiness would have been welcome. Still, Urie gives us a beautiful Richard, one the play deserves.

RICHARD II by William Shakespeare; Directed and Adapted by Craig Baldwin.

With: Michael Urie, Grantham Coleman, Ron Canada, Kathryn Meisle, David Mattar Merten, Lux Pascal, James Seol, Daniel Stewart Sherman, Ryan Spahn, Emily Swallow, Sarin Monae West.

Sets by Arnulfo Maldonado. Costumes by Rodrigo Muñoz. Sound by Brandon Wolcott.

Now playing through November 30 at Astor Place Theatre, 434 Lafayette St. Tickets available here.

Running time: 2 hours and 30 minutes, including one 15-minute intermission.

title.rendered: The Burning Cauldron of Fiery Fire

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

Anne Washburn’s new and very abstract comedy, The Burning Cauldron of Fiery Fire, asks a number of heated questions. Can a solid cast hold together a play which is built to come apart? The answer, happily, is yes. How does a small hen lay a human-size egg? Weird puppetry abounds in this joint production from The Vineyard Theatre and The Civilians. And can one man’s death change the nature of the community he lived in? Apparently so, though it is an open question whether that change is for the better.

The community Washburn introduces us to is no average suburb. Rather, it is a commune of adults and children who display, at times, cult-like tendencies. Living off the grid somewhere in California, they seem firmly anti-government and anti-technology, while being gently religious and hard-working. They farm their land when not putting on puppet pageants, and they keep secrets together when not having spats. They are a chosen family who have turned away from their biological roots.They also transform into a creepy chorus that chant evocative sentence fragments like, “Artichokes, pumpkins/Thistles/Great Horned Owl.” 

As directed by Steve Cosson, a cast of eight portray ten adults and eight kids. A large though unseen pig plays a prominent role, and the titular cauldron is made manifest but is up for interpretation. Is it a pathway to reincarnation? The gateway to Hell? There is little in terms of forthright explanation or revelatory backstory, and what narration there is comes from Milo (Bobby Moreno), sometimes as a wizened adult, sometimes as a put-upon 8-year-old, but first as a bratty troublemaker testing the boundaries of the adults around him. After ruining a painting created by one of the grown-ups, he confesses to the audience, “If I acted like an angel, an artist, I knew I could get away with pretty much anything.” For most of this production it feels as if Washburn is thinking the same thing.

Milo’s demeanor changes when that adult, Peter (Tom Pecinka), apparently commits suicide. It probably wasn’t the vandalized painting that drove him to it. It might have been the inability to cope with an upcoming inheritance or, in the semi-magical state the play skitters through, it might have been a glass of poisoned wine. For Milo and his kiddie pals, Peter’s demise is an adventure in bringing back the dead that involves saving a piglet who is carrying around Peter’s soul. For the adults, Peter’s death is first a matter of ritual then, after a not totally successful attempt at cremation, it is an exercise in lying, especially when Peter’s brother, Will (Pecinka), shows up in search of his sibling. 

Rituals and ceremonies are seemingly the lifeblood of this community yet they cannot get through saying grace around the dinner table without an interruption. And their most complicated ritual risks never reaching its end at all. This would be the pageant that Peter and the children had been creating before his death and which, performed as a play within a play, swallows up most of the second act. It is a fairy tale about a common man, also named Peter, whose true love for a princess allows him to escape the murderous intentions of the king, surviving deadly challenges three times. What Washburn is getting at with this shift in the action is again anybody’s guess: True love is a fantasy, perhaps, or that death is not as final as it seems. 

If sometimes confusing, the night is never dull thanks to the fully committed efforts of the cast. Especially fine is Bruce McKenzie as Thomas the sage, elder leader of the group and Bartley Booz as the mysterious Ghazal who either has an intellectual disability or an advanced understanding of primal nature. Meanwhile, Donnetta Lavinia Grays, as Diana, offers the best of the play’s many truisms when she observes, “Everyone wants to start a fire, no one wants to clear the ashes out in the morning.”

 

The Burning Cauldron of Fiery Fire – by Anne Washburn; directed by Steve Cosson

WITH: Jeff Biehl (Simon), Bartley Booz (Paul, Ghazal), Cricket Brown (Gracie), Donnetta Lavinia Grays (Diana), Bruce McKenzie (Thomas), Bobby Moreno (Milo), Tom Pecinka (Peter, Will) and Marianne Rendón (Mari). 

Andrew Boyce (Scenic Design), Emily Rebholz (Costume Design), Amith Chandrashaker (Lighting Design), Ryan Gamblin (Sound Design & Compositions), Tommy Kurzman (Wig & Hair Design), Monkey Boys Productions (Puppet Design). Vineyard Theatre, in co-production with The Civilians, 108 E 15th St., https://vineyardtheatre.org. Through November 30. Running time: 2 hours 5 minutes

title.rendered: A Symphony of Soul: Holland-Dozier-Holland’s Timeless Tribute at the 92nd Street Y

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

There are evenings in New York when music transcends mere entertainment, reconstructing memory itself and drawing listeners into a vivid chiaroscuro where joy, longing, and cultural history intermingle. Saturday evening’s presentation of “Motown’s Heat Wave: The Songs of Holland-Dozier-Holland” at The 92nd Street Y, as part of the Y’s Lyrics and Lyricists American Songbook Series, transformed the David Geffen Stage at Kaufmann Concert Hall into a sanctuary of American musical genius. In this space, the ephemeral becomes eternal through performance.

The Visual and Sonic Architecture of Detroit’s Soul

Under the masterful musical guidance of Michael O. Mitchell, this Lyrics & Lyricists celebration became an effervescent homage to a triumvirate whose songs shaped America’s sonic identity. The evening unfolded as a journey through continuity and nostalgia, tracing how the Holland-Dozier-Holland sound emerged from close-knit Detroit neighborhoods where church music, community rituals, and the collective heartbeat of soul nurtured an entirely new musical idiom.

The stage design, crafted by projection artists Kylee Loera and Taylor Gordon, created a kaleidoscope of eras—Detroit streets, recording studios, and civil-rights-era imagery dissolved into contemporary celebrations, suggesting how music transcends temporal boundaries. John Kelly’s lighting design operated as a visual counterpoint, sculpting the stage in warm golds and vibrant reds, illuminating not merely performers but emotional landscapes shifting from amber nostalgia to crystalline present joy.

L-R: Elizabeth Addison, Writer. Courtesy elizabethspeaks.com., Ehpraim Sykes. Performing Artist. Courtesy @ephsykes on Instagram, Curtis Wiley, Performing Artist, Courtesy @curtis_wiley on Instagram

Broadway Luminaries Channel Motown’s Spirit

What Brian Harlan Brooks achieved as director and choreographer, alongside writer Elizabeth Addison, was theatrical alchemy. The five featured vocalists—Derrick Baskin, Najah Hetsberger, Melrose Johnson, Ephraim Sykes, and Curtis Wiley—formed a sparkling ensemble whose theatrical vigor, charm, dancing, singing, and rhythmic precision galvanized the audience from the opening gesture.

Baskin, a Grammy and Tony nominee and “Ain’t Too Proud” alumnus, infused “Standing in the Shadow of Love” with a narrative arc that felt freshly dramaturgical, while later transforming “Bernadette” into a dramatic monologue. Hetsberger, currently gracing Broadway in “SIX,” channeled Diana Ross with such authenticity that one experienced the aura of the original. At the same time, her “Reach Out and Touch (Somebody’s Hand)” sparkled with playful urgency and translucent phrasing. Johnson shaped “You Keep Me Hangin’ On” with balletic poise, transforming the familiar lament into a declaration of joyous personal sovereignty.

Sykes, another Tony and Grammy nominee and “Ain’t Too Proud” alumnus, brought “I Can’t Help Myself” to a musical climax of emotional immediacy, creating a dialogue reminiscent of the call-and-response traditions from which this music emerged. Wiley’s tender and buoyant “Baby I Need Your Loving” revealed an artist deeply attuned to the melodic chiaroscuro that defines Holland-Dozier-Holland’s writing.

The Orchestra as Historical Narrator and Rhythmic Engine

Mitchell’s sextet functioned as both engine and aura; their sound was gloriously reminiscent of Motown’s legendary Funk Brothers yet unmistakably contemporary. Trumpeter Jeremiah Flack and trombonist Taja Graves-Parker supplied buoyant brass sonorities with rich exclamations and soaring lines. Guitarist Sherrod Barnes added rhythmic grit and eloquence, while bassist Chelton Grey grounded the ensemble with supple propulsion. DaiQuain Davis’s drums stitched everything together with precision and flair, creating what one might call the theater of the pulse—music so rhythmically alive that the audience couldn’t help but tap, clap, and sway.

Mitchell’s piano served as both anchor and catalyst, driving the narrative forward while honoring the music’s gospel roots, creating a shimmering effect where the present moves through the past.

Love as Revolutionary Act During Turbulent Times

Perhaps most profound was the evening’s revelation of how Holland-Dozier-Holland, during an era of Vietnam War upheaval and social fragmentation, chose love as their primary subject. As Mitchell noted in his program reflections, “their genius rested in discipline married to soulfulness, hooks balanced by humanity.” This wasn’t escapism but revolutionary optimism—the insistence on human connection when society seemed to be pulling apart.

Songs like “Reach Out I’ll Be There” and “You Can’t Hurry Love” became philosophical statements about patience, persistence, and the transformative power of human connection. Each lyric holds a kernel of universal longing: the desire to be loved, to break free, to hold on, to let go. These songs endure because they articulate the fragility and essentiality of human love.

L-R: Melrose Johnson, Performing Artist. Courtesy @melrosejohnsonvoice on Instagram, Derrick Baskin, Performing Artist. Courtesy @derrick.baskin on Instagram, Najah Hetsberger, Performing Artist. Courtesy @_only_one_najah on Instagram

A Communal Celebration of Cultural Memory

The evening’s true triumph lay in its dissolution of the fourth wall through rhythmic attraction. The audience—young, old, multigenerational—became part of the performance, embodying the recreation of cultural memory through collective participation when the whole company closed with “Heat Wave,” the hall transformed into a joyous celebration, audience members arising to spontaneous ovation.

Production stage manager Lori Wekselblatt and artistic producer Stephanie Alvarado Prugh orchestrated seamless transitions that maintained the evening’s vivacious momentum. At the same time, the design never overpowered the performers but intensified the emotional topography, guiding the audience through each song’s narrative terrain.

The Enduring Legacy of Holland-Dozier-Holland

This musical production, shimmering with humor, heart, and historical reverence, embodied the spirit Holland-Dozier-Holland championed: music as a catalyst of love, empathy, and connection. More than a nostalgic celebration, it was cultural archaeology, revealing how three songwriters from Detroit created a musical language that continues speaking across generations, races, and nations—a soul that found its voice and gifted it to the world.

In a few words, this concert was a joyous, soul-stirring celebration that transformed Kaufmann Concert Hall into a collective dance party of shared memory, where Broadway brilliance met Motown magic to create an evening of pure, irrepressible delight.

Prince Faggot at Studio Seaview Announces Third and Final Extension, Through December 13, Due To Demand
Prince Faggot is a beguiling tragicomedy.  “Beguiling” – I don’t often use that word, but it is the one that surfaced. Jordan Tannahill’s play is a dense tapestry of wonder, imagination, sexuality, humor and stinging observation.
Read our review HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Straight from an Alice + Olivia-esque dream closet and apartment they cohabit, Romy (Laura Bell Bundy) & Michele (Kara Lindsay) are high school best friends, fashionistas, and prepping to attend their 10-year reunion. While their peers from the 80’s now fall into the labels of entrepreneurs, wealthy, or pregnant, Romy and Michele feel pressured to fit in and be cool: the level of cool that they never quite seemed to reach in high school.

I’m sure you’ve been there: reunion suddenly is here and we want to see where everyone is–where they’ve made it–but ultimately, we want to one-up them. Romy and Michele wants everyone to know they’ve made it; they’ve made something of themselves.

The only problem is that Romy and Michele are a cashier and an unemployed salesgirl. Even Jordan Kai Burnett, emo outcast, has become an inventor, and Sandy–“The Frinkazoid” (Michael Thomas Grant) has developed into an extremely wealthy and attractive bachelor.

The plot of Romy & Michele: The Musical is a classic that has been a dozen times through film and stage: the popular clique that bullies the unpopular girls. And then you have the ripped jocks for which both groups of girls are vying (or dreaming of). But this hilariously relatable yet exaggerated production is immediately set apart from any other desperate-to-fit-in story.

Romy and Michele are already the coolest girls on stage–and they might completely fabricate an entire life of “success”–before they finally come to realize their worth and how their passion for fun and fashion can impact the lives of those around them.

Photo by Valerie Terranova

I do wish we’d dive deeper into this passion for fashion that’s put on full display in their reprise “This Is It (A Look They’ve Never Seen)” and their closing number “Changing the World (One outfit at a Time) because I love where the two girls ended up–together–but their conclusion was unexpected. I didn’t feel like I had been along for the ride of that part of their journey. Like, R & M?! Such a perfect conclusion that ties everything together and envelops their fashion that has always hinted at setting them apart, but there was a missed opportunity of leaning into their passion for this industry.

I am completely obsessed with the costuming. Thank you Tina McCartney for this curated wardrobe that was a joy in itself to admire. Maybe straight from the 90’s but it’s vibrant, fun, and so in style now. Feathers, pinks and purples and baby blues, pumps, and sequins. I want it all, and I felt like I was right there with the entire cast, thanks to this creative team–

Je’Shaun Jackson. Photo by Valerie Terranova

The projection work of this production is absolutely incredible. I am immediately immersed in high school hallways, on the dance floor, in a school cafeteria, in Romy and Michele’s apartment, and driving down the dessert roads in a Jaguar. When the curtain closes for intermission, I can’t tell what of the backdrop is digital and what’s not. This is the most striking and immersive set and projection work I have seen all season, by far.

While the projections and set was my most memorable aspect of this production, I can’t tell you how impressive the chemistry and vocals amongst the cast is. They are all queens. From Toby (Je’Shaun Jackson) and Jordan Kai Burnett taking over the stage, to the iconic duo of Laura Bell Bundy and Kara Lindsay, every number was consistent with the tone of the show.

Jordan Kai Burnett. Photo by Valerie Terranova

The “popular girls” also play background actors, which is confusing at points; I expect them to have the same negative relationship with Romy and Michele, but then they don’t (because they’re playing other women while dressed in the same style as their main characters). Simply changing their prep-girl clothing style would have deterred my confusion. A similar confusion occurred with one or two men that seemed to be playing other classmates (one styled as a western cowboy) whom I do not recall seeing at all in their high school era. But honestly, these were the only moments that paused me for a few seconds–

The audience for Romy & Michele was a complete raucous—literally! Endless laughter, clapping, and an audience member who was so rowdy that I couldn’t stop laughing at his wild excitement for the cast on stage, that it just all culminated into the most energy-packed night at the theater that I’ve had in a long time. Truly, an all-around fun production for all generations–not just those that can jam to the tunes of the 80’s and 90’s. I noticed several preteens in the audience, along with the adults whooping and cheering as their nostalgic music filled the theater during the pre-show music and intermission.

Romy & Michele:The Musical is stupid in all the right ways. The audience absolutely eats this up.

Based on the cult film classic Romy & Michele’s High School Reunion, the musical features an iconic duo that will make you buckle over in your seat laughing; I recommend everyone to go see this musical at Studio 42. Whether you’ve seen the movie or not, this musical adaptation will leave you in a brighter place.

Book by Robin Schiff; Music & Lyrics by Gwendolyn Sanford and Brandon Jay. Directed by Kristin Hanggi.

CREATIVE TEAM: Keith Harrison Dworkin (Music supervision, arrangements, and orchestrations) and Karla Puno Garcia (choreography), Tina McCartney (Costume Designer), Sheela Ramesh (Music Director, Keyboard/Conductor), Jason Sherwood (Scenic Designer), Jason Lyons (Lighting Designer), Connor Wang (Sound Designer), Caite Hevner (Projection Designer), Tommy Kurzman (Wig/Hair & Makeup Designer), Andrew Diaz (Props Designer), Kristy Norter (Music Coordinator).

CAST: Laura Bell Bundy (Romy White), Kara Lindsay (Michele Weinberger), Jordan Kai Burnett (Heather /others), DeMarius R. Copes (DJ/others), Ninako Donville (Lisa/others), Erica Dorfler (Kelly /others), Michael Thomas Grant (Sandy/others), Je’Shaun Jackson (Toby/others), Pascal Pastrana (Billy /others), and Lauren Zakrin (Christie/others).

Romy & Michele: The Musical is playing at Stage 42, 422 W 42nd St, New York, NY. Tickets can be purchased here.

title.rendered: Forever and a Day at UNDER St. Marks Theater

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Tonight was a meditation on love, memory, and the fragile geometry of human connection.

Under the low vaulted ceiling of Under St. Marks Theater, that tiny East Village crucible where Off-Broadway dreams are tested by intimacy, playwright Duran Arturo Lucio unfurled a work as delicate as the wingbeat of a cardinal and as unflinching as grief itself. His play, Forever and a Day, presented by FRIGID New York during its Days of the Dead Festival, is more than a tale of remembrance—it is an ethical inquiry into what remains of love when time and mortality have had their say.

The Setting and the Tone

The evening begins, appropriately, in music. Audiences are greeted by the melancholic pulse of “Nunca Tristes (Me Vale Madre)” by Renee, the yearning of Paloma Morphy’s “Mefaltas Tú,” and Kevin Kaarl’s “San Lucas.” These songs summon a mood of Latin American fatalism tempered by joy—an emotional chiaroscuro preparing us for Lucio’s blend of humor and heartbreak.

Director Billy Luce-Murray uses the confined black-box space to heighten the sense of participation: the audience feels less like spectators and more like fellow mourners in a church basement. What might have been a funeral becomes a “celebration of life,” an act of communal witness for Tom, a young man who has taken his own life. Tom’s four pals who gather—Allen, Christina, Laura, and Zander—are friends, hosts, and ghosts, haunted by their unfinished conversations with the dead.

The Architecture of Memory

Lucio, who first conceived this play a decade ago in Dallas and has re-forged it for a New York audience, constructs the drama like a prism. Each scene refracts Tom’s death through a different emotional wavelength: Allen’s guilt-laden affection, Christina’s shy nostalgia, Laura’s familial fury, Zander’s pragmatic tenderness. The story unfolds in overlapping recollections—what might be called a series of concentric veracities—in which the truth is not revealed so much as earned.

Camron Alexander’s Allen anchors the play with a quiet, watchful grief that echoes the great realists of the British stage. We see him half-asleep, dodging calls from his mother, trying to keep his urban detachment intact until news of Tom’s death cracks the armor. Sean Morillo gives Tom a spectral presence: not a vengeful ghost but a Socratic conscience who returns only to provoke questions. When he appears to Allen in fleeting visions, the audience feels that cherished theatrical miracle—the transformation of private despair into shared illumination.

Thematic Undercurrents

At its core, Forever and a Day examines how modern life both connects and isolates us. Lucio’s characters have escaped a small conservative hometown for the big city, yet find themselves captive to new forms of alienation—corporate cubicles, dating apps, the relentless demand to perform stability. Their memorial for Tom becomes a reckoning with their own vanishing certainties.

Ana Armenta as Laura threads the piece with luminous sincerity. Her bilingual outbursts in Spanish—sometimes prayers, sometimes curses—inject rhythm and cultural texture, reminding us that identity is a language of inheritance. Kamila Kopcová as Christina begins as comic relief—self-absorbed, distracted, delightfully incongruous—but her façade crumbles to reveal a deep, almost mystical empathy. Victor Gao completes the quartet with understated warmth; he listens, which in this play is a radical act.

Lucio’s dramaturgy recalls Chekhov’s humane attention to what is not said. Every joke conceals a tremor of loss. Every silence lengthens like a moral question. And yet, as in G. B. Shaw’s best social comedies, the play refuses despair. Its laughter is the sound of endurance.

Days of the Dead Festival. Courtesy @frigidnewyork on Instagram

Craft and Design

Stage manager Winnie Chiang coordinates a minimalist world: a few folding chairs, dim candlelight, snacks, and raffle tickets—tokens of normalcy that feel absurdly poignant. Lighting transitions blur dream and recollection; sound cues glide from pop melancholy and sentiment to sacred hush. The effect is chamber theater of rare concentration.

Lucio’s language alternates between lyrical monologue and clipped dialogue, balancing poetry with the matter-of-fact. When Laura recalls her brother Tom comparing life to “a mother bird with two chicks, one vanished,” the image becomes the play’s central metaphor: love as care despite inevitability.

In one of the evening’s most striking moments, Christina speaks of her favorite bird—the cardinal, symbol of persistence and visitation. When a red light sweeps across the stage, we feel Tom’s spirit not as supernatural fancy but as emotional continuity. The dead live on, Lucio implies, in our capacity to keep asking why.

Philosophical Resonances

Where one might dissect moral pretenses with dialectic wit, Lucio probes our evasions of vulnerability. He suggests that mourning is not backward-looking but an ethical act in the present. The celebration of life becomes a manifesto for empathy in a culture numbed by irony.

Arguably, theater should bring the unseen moral forces to vision. Here, those forces are loneliness, cultural displacement, and the fragile hope of love. Lucio gives them body and voice. The play’s denouement—no spoilers—binds its characters through forgiveness, hope, and aptly limited resolution. The audience leaves not with answers but with a renewed appetite for compassion.

Forever and a Day at UNDER St. Marks Theater

CAST

  • Camron Alexander – Allen
  • Sean Morillo – Tom
  • Kamila Kopcová – Christina
  • Ana Armenta – Laura
  • Victor Gao – Zander

ARTISTIC

  • Playwright: Duran Arturo Lucio
  • Director: Billy Luce-Murray
  • Producer: Ana Armenta
  • Stage Manager: Winnie Chiang

Running seventy-five minutes without intermission, Forever and a Day is a compact triumph of sincerity over cynicism. It reaffirms FRIGID New York’s mission to offer an inclusive platform for emerging voices and reminds us that profound theater can arise from the smallest of rooms.

Under St. Mark’s Theater
94 St. Marks Place, New York, NY 10009
Presented by FRIGID New York
Click for Tickets | Runtime 75 minutes | No intermission

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“Love your bat boy.”

A bald head, pointy ears, and a thirst for blood. We all want a cute bat boy. And this Bat Boy, Taylor Trensch, is fresh off a Tony-nominated run in Floyd Collins.

Hold me, Bat Boy!

Touch me, Bat Boy!

…

Love me, Bat Boy!

Save me, Bat Boy!

Make it all turn out all right!

Bat Boy: The Musical is a horror comedy full of absurdity that will give you the whole range of emotions. I’m on the edge of my seat longing for a bat boy; I’m ferociously picking my nails off in fear and worry for the hate that this small West Virginia town has for Bat Boy. Town Veterinarian and father Christopher Sieber has quite a complicated relationship with his new “son.” We’re taken into a church service, where we transition from grunge and rock to gospel. I find short-lived relief, in church with Reverend Hightower’s (Jacob Ming-Trent) convincing for the town to give Bat Boy a chance, after this haf human-half bat drops down to his knees in desire, longing, and repentance. This half-bat-half-boy may be impossible to breed, but he’s very real in front of me, and I find myself taking his living very seriously.

Photo by Joan Marcus

Bat Boy just wants to find where he comes from, who he is; he wants to find his home. He’s emotional and naive. I’m hesitant with his presence, much like the small town in this cruel world. But unlike their want to kill this unnatural and dangerous creature, I very quickly warm up to the boy within the bat-like appearance and mannerisms.

Taylor Trensch embodies this human-animal so well, mastering these creepy but simultaneously angelic movements across the stage. I could watch him hang on beams, scurry on all fours,and  leap over a couch for hours.

With a handful of familiar faces, this cast unites on City Center’s stage, taking a break from their regular productions to bring us Bat Boy: The Musical. Months after closing as an infamous dead outlaw-corpse, we see Andrew Durand die again, this time from a poison and giant needle. But, as expected, he plays that southern bad boy character too well. On a break from Heathers The Musical, Kerry Butler plays the mother of Shelley and protector of Bat Boy, but just nearly 25 years prior, she originated the Broadway role of teen daughter and blossoming love interest of Bat Boy, Shelley Parker. This time around, at New York City Center, among the rest of this star-studded cast, Shelley is played by Gabi Carrubba.

Photo by Joan Marcus

Bat Boy: The Musical is equally heartfelt as it is comedic and horrific. From deep fisting a cow center stage, breaking a bunny’s neck to suck down its blood, animal intercourse in a forest which leads to Shelley and Bat Boy’s own animalistic behavior, this performance does not disappoint in morbid and dark humor.

Bat Boy just wants to fit in, but after coming from a cave, he needs to learn (in a comically distinguished British accent) how to talk and act in a community. joining his new family for breakfast and garnering the respect of his entire host-family is a feat in itself, but we quickly see him flourish in catching onto mannerisms and conversation. Mom Meredith babies Bat Boy, like any biological mom would baby a malnourished, innocent son, and I was fearful of some mother-son romantic relationship in development. But, alas, a twincest does seem like a much unexpected, wilder obstacle to get over for Bat Boy.

Photo by Joan Marcus

Aside from the mastery of each character’s incarnation and equally memorable vocals of the restored musical numbers, the eerie but contemporary set breathes the dark, moist, and obscure feels of this piece to the theater.

In the middle of spooky season, catch this unrestrained and wild musical return to New York City; it captures the dark insanity and hilarious eccentricity all while exhibiting a top-notch cast, vocals, and orchestrations.

Book by Keythe Farley & Brian Flemming; Music and Lyrics by Laurence O’Keefe.

Original Arrangements and Orchestrations by Alex Lacamoire and Laurence O’Keefe.

CAST: Kerry Butler (Meredith Parker), Gabi Carrubba (Shelley Parker), Andrew Durand (Rick Taylor), Mary Faber (Lorraine), Alan H Green (Bud), Evan Harrington (Ned), John-Michael Lyles (Ron Taylor), Tom McGowan (Sheriff Reynolds), Jacob Ming-Trent (Reverend Hightower), Alex Newell (The God Pan), Olivia Puckett (Ruthie Taylor), Marissa Rosen (Daisy), Christopher Sieber (Dr. Parker), Taylor Trensch (Bat Boy), Colin Trudell (Charley), Rema Webb (Maggie), and Marissa Jaret Winokur (Mrs. Taylor).

ORCHESTRA: Andrew Resnick (Music Director, Conductor/Keyboard), Daniel Green (Associate Music Director), Kimberlee Wertz (Music Coordinator), Josh Clayton (Director of Music Administration & Score Restoration), Mike Pettry (Keyboard/Guitars), Dillon Kondor (Guitars), Rob Jost (Bass), James Eblen (Drums), Andy Blanco (Percussion), Julie Pacheco (Reeds), Alden Banta (Reeds), Trevor Neumann (Trumpet)

Bat Boy: The Musical is playing as a limited-engagement run at New York City Center, 131 West 55th Street, New York, NY, until Nov. 9. Run time is 2 hours and 15 minutes, with one intermission. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

When I first saw the title of this play and knew it was about immigrants I thought “Queens” might be in reference to who these immigrants were in a figurative sense.

It’s not.  It’s Queens – you know that borough over there. The one with all the immigrants. The one that I will never think of the same way again.

Martyna Majok has written a play that may shatter you as it did me, but don’t let that deter you from going to this production.  Hey – we all need a little shattering.  We need a little shake-up.  We need a little of “Look at it this way.”  This would be the place for all that.

Here is what happened to me.  I think of myself as a very liberal white woman who treats people with respect.  I was disabused of this notion several months ago when I was told by one of my neighbors that I was in fact an inconsiderate white woman.  We never got to resolve this situation but did make it back to being on cordial terms.  Still, I wonder, who else of my acquaintances thinks I am an inconsiderate white woman, and are they right?  Sometimes I think yes and other times no.

What this play did was renforce the idea that treating people with respect is not enough.  In the case of immigrants: people who come here leave people they love behind.  They come here to create a new life that is light years away from home.  They come here because staying back there has too little to offer that is good and plenty that is bad.  That man is more than your smiling bus boy.  That woman is more than the woman offering candy bars on the subway.  They are solar systems with stories to tell.

“Queens” does not point a finger at anyone, and at the same time it points a finger at everyone.  A total of eight women who at one time or another live in a basement apartment in Queens.  They are from Poland, Ukraine, Belarus, Afghanistan, and Honduras.  How they find this apartment is not as important as the fact that they do.  All the women speak English on purpose to keep up their language skills as well as to remind them of where they are.

Where they are is not home.

They have run away from home to find a place where they can earn enough money to send back to the people they left behind.  They are refugees, like Ms. Majok is herself.  The stories are told without sentiment.  Women are vulnerable, and this apartment provides them with safety which is crucial.  Their stories spin out like spider webs that swing out and around, slowly encompassing them all, whether they want to be caught or not.

We watch as the facts are laid out in patches.  The time stretches over 16 years.  This element of the play I found confusing because there is little information to help locate the action as the scenes change.  Perhaps the author did this on purpose so that we become  a bit lost like these women.  For me, it would have been helpful to have projections – as I have seen in many a production – giving us the year and location.  As it was, this lack of information was distracting.

The show does not suffer much from this omission.  The characters slip back and forth like chameleons.  Not only do they move through time, they also move through several languages.  Because we don’t have an exact bead on whence each character comes we can only know they are not speaking English – and what a time this incredible ensemble has with this language free-for-all.  A quick glance through my Playbill didn’t tell me if anyone was bilingual – and if they are not, these folks deserve a medal for making us believe they were.

“Queens” is an ambitious play that begs us to look twice at immigrants.  Look at them the way we would want to be looked at.

Yeah – go get shattered.

Queens, written by Martyna Majok, directed by Trip Cullman.

WITH  Brooke Bloom, Anna Chlumsky, Sharlene Cruz, Marin Ireland, Julia Lester, Nadine Malouf, Andrea Syglowski, Nicole Villamil.

Scenic Design by Marsha Ginsberg, Lighting Design by Ben Stanton, Costume Design by Sarah Laux, Dialect Coach Jane Guyer Fujita

Through December 7 at Manhattan Theatre Club.  Tickets HERE

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

The Yellow Wallpaper, a short story by Charlotte Perkins Gilman written in 1892, is an early expose’ into the world of women’s rights as we were (and still are in most of the world) thought of and treated as second class citizens. Gilman’s classic is the story of a young mother Jane (Megan Ort), her doctor husband, John (Josh Andrés Rivera) and sister-in-law, Jennie, (Paloma D’Auria) moving into a somewhat run down summer mansion for two months so that Jane, a new mother, can have time to herself to get over her anxieties after the birth of her child. Her doctor/husband, believes, as the educated man he is, that he knows what’s best for his fragile anxious wife. His sister, Jennie, who acts as the baby’s nanny while Jane gets her much needed quiet and rest, is tolerant of her sister-in-law, but that is all – tolerant. The wallpaper in the room Jane is put in is old, fading, a yellow mash of paper that is peeling in many areas. If you look at something for long enough, it begins to take on a life of its own, and so the wallpaper slowly begins to move. Over the course of the two months the one-room solitary confinement proves for Jane only to exasperate her fragility. She sees in the wallpaper a woman trapped, she sees women trapped and trying to crawl out. A beautiful and horrifying metaphor. Solitary confinement IS the cause of suicide, the cause of decline in emotional sickness. But all of that is pushed aside as the husband knows best.

In sisters Caitlin Ort and Megan Ort’s presentation of The Yellow Wallpaper, they beautifully show the decline of a woman trying to do as her husband prescribes, believing that HE knows what is best for her. “What is best for her,” a constant phrase by a self-absorbed man. The only man on the premises and thus the lord to all.

This dance-theater adaptation is so splendid in its staging utilizing the talents of three wonderful dancers (Maya Musial, Annie Sherman, Claire van Bever) who in costume and movement, are shadows come to life. They cover the boundaries of the room until they take over the room and its single inhabitant.

All of the performers are marvelous. Director Caitlin Ort creates a piece whose ending will take your breath away. In this tremendous adaptation Jane is diving into the world she absolutely knows through her hallucinations, to be real, with confidence, joy and conviction, finally she sees an end to her maladies, embracing the wallpaper and those who populate it. And in a sense, embracing herself.

All the artists give strong performances in this 90-minute jump into Gilman’s world of 1892.

Caitlin’s direction along with Megan’s choreography have created inspiring, haunting, vigorous and exceptional moments in the telling of Jane’s fall.

For me what did not hold up as well – the lighting. Most of it is bewitching, when needed stark and glaring. All of it worked to help create the tone and mood of the scene until it went to the split seconds of blackout for the actors to move or to show us time had moved. Blackouts for me create split seconds where you lose the audience. With lighting and stage movement there are so many choices to create a smooth and interesting transition of time that does not go to black.

Personally, I kept thinking as I watched the evening unfold that this was Gilman’s way of showing a woman’s dive into what we now know as postpartum depression, something that was not considered in the 19th century.

The Yellow Wallpaper Written by  Charlotte Perkins Gilman, adaptation by Caitlin Ort and Megan Ort, Director/Choreographer – Caitlin Ort, and Associate Director/Choreographer – Megan Ort.

With: Megan Ort, Josh Andrés Rivera, Paloma D’Auria, Maya Musial, Annie Sherman, and Claire van Bever

Creative Team:  Caitlin Ort and Megan Ort, Director/Choreographer – Caitlin Ort, and Associate Director/Choreographer – Megan Ort. Director/choreographer, Kyra Leeds Assistant Director, Morgan Blanchard Assistant Choreographer, Alexa Powell Assistant Stage Manager , Sari Stifelman producer

The performances took place at Gibney: Agnes Varis Performing Arts Center, located at 280 Broadway (entrance at 53A Chambers St), New York, NY.

Running Time: 90 minutes no intermission

title.rendered: Marilyn Maye at 54 Below Through November!!!

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

I am always prepared to weep when I am in the audience for Marilyn Maye.  It has gotten so serious that now I weep when she enters the room.  At 54 Below everyone in the audience is a beloved admirer.  Maye comes close to floating as she glides through the crowd and onto the stage.  There is no “off stage” for Maye.  Once Maye enters she is ON.  And once she steps up onto the stage with her trio – Musical Director Ted Firth, Tom Hubbard on Bass and Mark McClean on drums – all we can do is try and keep up.

This year marks the 100th birthday of Johhny Carson.  Maye appeared on his show 76 time, which I think is the record.  She sings several of his favorites and tells us that his favorite was “Here’s That Rainy Day.”  Tha man who made America laugh had a sweet sad side as well for his “Super Singer”.  In addition to Johnny, Maye mentions Steve Allen who discovered her performing in Kansas City and brought her to his show.

In other words, May wants us to know that she has been around.  Her age is 97.  Think about that one folks.  She had her debut at Carnegie Hall at the age of 95.  As she said – “it was about time – I had practiced enough.” Those of us who were fortunate enough to be there counted 16 standing ovations that did not slow her down one bit.

In case you think May could be a little old fashioned – think again.  She has a voice that carries to the heaves and makes it look easy.  Every bit of her is 100% heart,  She brings to the American songbook a life filled with a bunch of not so easy times.  Just as she was coming up the Beatles swept in and she was sidelined.  Not that she was stopped.  She kept on singing all over the country.

When Marilyn Maye sings “No Bad News,” you know it comes from years of figuring it out as she went along.

Thank the angels that she is finally here with us.

Maye is on an extended stay at 54 Below thought the end of November.  Schedule and ticket are HERE

Do not miss this show – you will never EVER regret being in the presence of this miracle called Marilyn.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.
