title.rendered: Virtuosi Violini and the American Classical Orchestra

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

There are evenings when time collapses and the boundaries between centuries dissolve like morning mist over the Venetian lagoon. Such was the enchantment wrought by the American Classical Orchestra on October 28, 2025, within the acoustically resplendent sanctuary of Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church. Indeed, this wasn’t merely a concert—it was a sonic séance, summoning the spirits of Italian Baroque masters with the kind of authenticity that would have made the most critical of audiences nod approvingly over a morning coffee.

Under the scholarly yet playful direction of Thomas Crawford, the evening unfolded as a carefully curated journey through the golden age of the violin concerto. Moreover, Crawford’s introductions to each work proved themselves to be miniature masterclasses in musical history, delivered with the wit of Victor Borge’s elegant spoofs and Peter Schickele’s immortal P.D.Q. Bach parodies. His erudition sparkled with humor, illuminating the context of each composition while never losing sight of the music’s essential humanity.

Maestro Thomas Crawford conducts the American Classical Orchestra in a concert entitled “Magnificently Mozart,” in Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall in New York City. Courtesy aconyc.org

The Doctrine of Affections Brought to Life

The program commenced with Giuseppe Brescianello’s Violin Concerto in G Major, Bre 9, featuring Chloe Fedor as violino principale. Fedor’s playing embodied the Baroque Doctrine of Affections with extraordinary precision—each movement maintaining its singular emotional character, whether jubilant or contemplative. Her tone, which The New York Times has praised as “lovely, plush, seductive,” captured the courtly elegance of works originally performed in the aristocratic salons of Württemberg, where Brescianello served as Kapellmeister.

Subsequently, Tomaso Albinoni’s Violin Concerto No. 12 in B-flat Major, Op. 10, showcased Edson Scheid‘s remarkable technical facility. The piece, likely commissioned for Venetian nobility, demonstrated the sophisticated interplay between soli (solo instruments), ripieno (full ensemble), and basso continuo—that essential foundation of harpsichord and bass described as the rhythmic and harmonic spine of Baroque music. Crawford’s harpsichord work, discreet yet indispensable, provided the rhythmic pulse binding these disparate voices into a cohesive whole.

L-R: Edson Scheid, Violin. Photo by Mei Stone. Aisslinn Nosky, Violin. Photo courtesy aisslinn.com

Tartini’s Mystical Depths and Bach’s Architectural Splendor

Transitioning to Giuseppe Tartini’s Violin Concerto in E Minor, D. 56, Augusta Lodge revealed depths of expression that seemed to channel the composer’s own legendary “Devil’s Trill” mysticism. As concertmaster of Les Arts Florissants, Lodge brought a superb commanding presence. Consequently, her interpretation demonstrated how Tartini’s works, originally performed at the Basilica di Sant’Antonio in Padua, were designed to move the soul through specific musical rhetorical devices.

Meanwhile, Johann Sebastian Bach’s famed Concerto for Two Violins in D Minor, BWV 1043 featured the dynamic pairing of Nosky and Fedor. Their dialogue resembled two streams of consciousness flowing in parallel, sometimes diverging, sometimes merging in unexpected pools of harmony. The ripieno section, comprising Jessica Troy and Kyle Miller on violas, Loretta O’Sullivan on cello, and John Feeney on bass, provided a foundation as sturdy as the Gothic arches of Leipzig’s Thomaskirche, where Bach himself once presided.

L-R: Loretta O’Sullivan, Cello. Photo by David Rodgers. Chloe Fedor, Violin. Courtesy chloefedorviolinist.com

We were also treated to an unannounced performance of a pensive segment from a Vivaldi work performed by solo cellist Loretta O’Sullivan with bass and continuo. Transcendent and elegiac.

Vivaldi’s Playful Audition and Crawford’s Comic Genius

One of the evening’s many delightful surprises arrived with Antonio Vivaldi’s Concerto for Four Violins in B Minor, RV 580, and a well-earned encore performance of “Autumn” from The Four Seasons. Here, Crawford’s theatrical gifts blazed forth. Having introduced Vivaldi’s dual roles as priest and maestro at Venice’s Ospedale della Pietà—that remarkable institution where orphaned and abandoned girls received world-class musical training—Crawford invited the audience to imagine “Autumn” as an audition for young musicians seeking positions in Vivaldi’s celebrated all-female orchestra.

ACO in a concert entitled Virtuosi Violini. Courtesy @americanclassicalorchestra on Instagram

As the musicians performed, Crawford interjected humorous asides from the harpsichord in the spirit of “glib glissandos,” “unvirtuous vibrato,” and “indignant crescendos” (my words)—the sorts of comments conductors typically mutter under their breath as they sneer at hapless musicians. This inspired bit of musical theater illuminated a historical truth: Vivaldi composed hundreds of works for his talented students, many of whom achieved international renown. The legendary Anna Maria dal Violin, for instance, inspired numerous concerti showcasing her virtuosic capabilities. Crawford’s commentary, while comic, honored the profound pedagogical relationship between the “Red Priest” and his remarkable students.

The Perfect Acoustic Canvas

Throughout the evening, the Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church provided an ideal setting for period instrument performance. Designed in 1899 by James E. Ware & Son and acoustically renovated in the late 1990s, the sanctuary’s marble surfaces and soaring vaulted ceiling created the kind of reverberation that early music demands. Furthermore, the church’s magnificent Casavant pipe organ, installed in 1962 and designed by the renowned organist Robert Baker, represents the venue’s commitment to musical excellence. Though silent this evening, its presence reminded us that this sacred space has long been a haven for historically informed performance.

L-R: Augusta McKay Lodge, Violin. Photo credits to Lauren Desberg and Kevin Condon. Jessica Troy, Viola. Courtesy aconyc.org

The ACO’s use of period instruments—wooden flutes, gut strings, valveless brass, and leather-headed timpani (just strings and harpsichord tonight)—produces timbres familiar to audiences in 18th-century Venice, Vienna, and Leipzig. Authentic instruments don’t merely recreate historical sounds; they reveal compositional choices that modern instruments often obscure. The natural blend of these instruments, their capacity for subtle dynamic shading, and their inherent clarity of line allowed the music’s rhetorical gestures to speak with unprecedented eloquence.

A Testament to Musical Time Travel

This concert exemplified all that makes the American Classical Orchestra indispensable to New York’s cultural landscape. Crawford and his superlative musicians don’t merely perform Baroque music; they inhabit it, understand it, and—most importantly—communicate its emotional truth to contemporary audiences. Their adherence to period performance practice, combined with Crawford’s infectious enthusiasm and pedagogical clarity, transforms each concert into both an entertainment and an education.

As the final notes of “Autumn” faded into the church’s reverberant space, one couldn’t help but reflect on Virginia Woolf’s observation that “the beauty of the world has two edges, one of laughter, one of anguish, cutting the heart asunder.” The ACO’s artistry navigates both edges with consummate skill, reminding us why these centuries-old compositions continue to speak to the human condition with undiminished power.

The American Classical Orchestra’s October concert at Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church delivered an extraordinary evening of Italian Baroque masterworks performed on period instruments with virtuosic scholarly precision, stunning artistry, and Thomas Crawford’s signature wit. Don’t miss their captivating 2025-26 season, which promises more historically informed performances that transport audiences across centuries.

L-R: Kyle Miller, Viola. Courtesy fournations.org. John Feeney, Bass. Courtesy aconyc.org

Virtuosi Violini and the American Classical Orchestra

For more insights into classical music performance and the power of period instruments, explore articles at Opening Night Online, where music criticism meets cultural commentary in sophisticated yet accessible prose.

title.rendered: The Truth About Transylvania: A Gothic Triumph at the Mezzanine Theatre

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

When memory becomes theatre, we discover Patricia Lynn’s audacious reimagining of the Dracula Myth in a meta-theatrical investigation.

A Critical Examination of Truth, Testimony, and Theatrical Transformation

In the hallowed tradition of theatrical innovation that has marked A.R.T./New York’s commitment to provocative dramaturgy, Patricia Lynn’s The Truth About Transylvania emerges as an extraordinary work of ambition and intellectual rigor. Under the astute direction of Jacob Titus, this world premiere at the Mezzanine Theatre achieves what few contemporary works dare attempt: a complete reconceptualization of the vampire myth through the lens of feminist epistemology and postmodern theatrical form.

As the audience settled in, they were wrapped in tone-setting music like “Paint it Black,” performed by Ciara, and “Bela Lugosi is Dead”, by CHVFCHES.

Lynn, who describes herself as a gothic feminist playwright, aims to reclaim the traditionalist genre by writing contemporary gothic plays that ask provocative questions about women and society today. This self-awareness manifests brilliantly in her latest work, which transforms Bram Stoker’s canonical text into a meta-theatrical investigation of truth, trauma, and the treacherous terrain of memory.

L-R: Mark Weatherup, Jr. Courtesy markweatherup.com. Patricia Lynn in a scene from The Truth About Transylvania. Courtesy patriciamlynn.com

The Architecture of Disbelief: A Theatrical Conceit

The production’s central conceit—a livestreamed testimony in which Jonathan Harker and his wife, Millie Bell, attempt to prove Count Dracula’s existence—represents a masterstroke of contemporary relevance. Mark Weatherup Jr.’s portrayal of John Harker transcends mere character work; it becomes an excavation of masculine vulnerability rarely witnessed on the American stage. His opening gambit with the “Truth Chair”—a familial instrument of patriarchal interrogation—establishes the production’s central dialectic between inherited authority and experiential knowledge.

Weatherup’s performance champions the kind of psychological realism that transforms melodrama into a serious artistic endeavor, never sacrificing intellectual complexity for emotional effect. When John confesses his complicity in Dracula’s escape—”I let him walk away. And I knew what he would do. How many people he’d… And I didn’t care”—Weatherup delivers these lines with a devastating quietude that recalls the finest moments of naturalistic drama. Here is acting that serves the dual purpose of entertainment and enlightenment, drawing audiences into moral complexities while maintaining theatrical vitality.

Miles Purinton as The Concierge, Patricia Lynn as Millie. Photo by Al Foote III.

The Feminist Reclamation: Millie Bell as Truth-Seeker

Patricia Lynn, performing her own creation as Millie Bell, embodies what might be termed the intellectual “life force” of the play. Her dual role as playwright-performer represents a theatrical audacity that recalls the tradition of artist-provocateurs who use the stage as a platform for both artistic expression and social commentary.

Lynn’s Millie is no mere victim awaiting rescue; she is an etymology-obsessed intellectual warrior, wielding language as both shield and weapon. Her monologue about childhood monsters and the dictionary—”I’d pick a word, any word. And I’d look up its etymology. I’d find its meaning. Which helped me find my meaning”—represents theatrical writing of the highest order. Furthermore, the character’s linguistic precision serves as a counterpoint to the epistemological uncertainty that pervades the narrative.

The play distinguishes itself by combining intellectual debate with theatrical entertainment. When Millie challenges the very premise of their testimonial enterprise—”Just because something feels real, feels true inside your head, your heart too, that doesn’t mean it’s the truth”—Lynn delivers a philosophical proposition that uses wit and dialectical reasoning to illuminate profound social questions while keeping audiences thoroughly engaged.

Miles Purinton as The Concierge, Patricia Lynn as Millie, and Mark Weatherup Jr. as John. Photo by Al Foote III.

The Villain as Vaudevillian: Van Helsing Reimagined

Miles Purinton’s interpretation of Van Helsing represents perhaps the production’s most radical departure from tradition. No longer the sage vampire hunter of Victorian lore, this Van Helsing emerges as a postmodern charlatan, a meta-theatrical manipulator whose repeated invocation of The Usual Suspects—”The greatest trick the devil pulled was convincing the world he did not exist”—becomes increasingly sinister with each iteration.

Moreover, Purinton navigates this complex characterization with remarkable dexterity, particularly in the climactic revelation scene where Van Helsing’s machinations are exposed. His delivery of the line “A man must do what a man must do, and if no one believes this man, he must go to extremes” carries echoes of Victorian masculinity’s destructive certainties, critiquing the very foundations of patriarchal authority with sardonic precision.

Dracula poster by Hamilton Deane & John L. Balderston 1938. Public Domain

The Monster in Shadows: David Israeli’s Enigmatic Count

David Israeli’s Count Dracula presents a fascinating theatrical paradox: a presence felt most powerfully in absence. Israeli’s largely wordless performance relies on physicality and atmosphere, creating what might be termed a negative space around which the other characters orbit. Subsequently, his few verbal exchanges—delivered through an ingenious vocal displacement technique that echoes from all corners of the theater—transform simple greetings into ontological threats.

The scene where Dracula presents his “homework” to John—a melancholic essay about loving “the shadow, the shade”—provides Israeli with his most substantial dramatic moment. Consequently, the actor invests these simple words with centuries of existential weight, suggesting depths that the play’s meta-theatrical framework simultaneously reveals and conceals.

Mark Weatherup Jr. as John. Photo by Al Foote III.

Technical Mastery in Service of Thematic Complexity

The production’s technical elements deserve particular commendation. Austin Boyle’s lighting design creates a chiaroscuro effect that would have delighted the Symbolists, while Randall Benichak’s sound design—particularly the recurring wolf howls that only certain characters can hear—adds layers of psychological uncertainty to an already complex narrative structure.

Additionally, Al Foote III’s fight choreography achieves a balletic violence that serves the play’s thematic concerns about complicity and action. The climactic double stabbing of Van Helsing—Millie with her stake, John with his pen—becomes a potent visual metaphor for the intersection of feminine agency and masculine tradition.

Stage manager Heather Olmstead orchestrates these elements with invisible precision, maintaining the production’s breakneck pace while allowing moments of genuine emotional resonance to breathe.

Philosophical Depths and Theatrical Heights

What elevates The Truth About Transylvania beyond mere clever deconstruction is Lynn’s genuine engagement with fundamental questions of epistemology and ethics. The play’s exploration of testimony, truth, and trauma resonates with contemporary concerns about narrative authority and believability, particularly in cases of gendered violence.

Lynn’s writing style, compared to the Brontë sisters’, creates stories of passion, love, and morality that carry the realism of our time while remaining ageless. This Gothic sensibility, filtered through a distinctly 21st-century consciousness, produces moments of startling theatrical power.

Furthermore, the production exemplifies how contemporary theater can transform from mere entertainment into a serious artistic and intellectual endeavor, addressing social consciousness through clever language and wit while educating, challenging, and enlightening audiences. The play’s treatment of the vampire myth as a metaphor for patriarchal violence and gaslighting achieves this dual purpose brilliantly. Yet Lynn never allows didacticism to overwhelm dramatic necessity; the play remains, at its core, a gripping theatrical experience.

Couverture de la première édition française du roman de Bram Stoker, Dracula. L’Homme de la nuit, Paris, L’Édition française illustrée, Collection littéraire des romans étrangers.
Illustration de Pierre Falké. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Contemporary Resonance and Classical Structure

The genius of Lynn’s construction lies in its simultaneous embrace and subversion of classical dramatic unities. While the action unfolds in real time during a single livestream session, the narrative spirals across multiple temporal planes—from the couple’s traumatic vacation in Romania to John’s imprisonment in Castle Dracula, from childhood memories to present-day reckonings.

This temporal fluidity serves the play’s central investigation of memory’s reliability. When John admits he cannot remember how he escaped the castle or returned to Millie, the admission becomes more than a plot device—it transforms into a meditation on trauma’s effect on narrative coherence. Subsequently, the audience must grapple with the same uncertainties that plague the characters: What constitutes proof? Whose testimony carries authority? Can truth exist independent of belief?

The production operates on the principle that theater should present ideas through dramatic conflict rather than clear moral absolutes. The villain proves as conscientious as the hero, if not more so, raising the essential question of which character truly represents good or evil. This moral complexity, presented through sophisticated dialogue and intellectual rigor, marks the work as belonging to the tradition of serious modern drama.

The Language of Modern Gothic

Lynn’s dialogue achieves that rare theatrical alchemy where intellectual sophistication meets emotional authenticity. Characters speak with grammatical diversity and varied accents, reflecting the many ways we navigate the English language. The text possesses an almost musical quality—a joyousness in language that elevates even the darkest moments with linguistic playfulness.

Consider John’s confession about his father: “He invited Millie over. Sat her down in that stupid Truth Chair of his. Cross-examined her like she was a hostile witness.” The colloquial “stupid” colliding with the formal legal terminology creates a linguistic tension that mirrors the character’s psychological state. This attention to vocal texture and rhythm transforms exposition into an aria, argument into a duet.

David Israeli as The Count, Mark Weatherup Jr. as John. Photo by Al Foote III.

A Testament to Off-Broadway’s Vitality

The production exemplifies the vital role that Off-Broadway continues to play in American theater. Unencumbered by commercial pressures that might demand a more conventional treatment of the Dracula myth, A.R.T./New York Theatres has provided Lynn and her collaborators the freedom to experiment, to provoke, and ultimately to triumph.

A.R.T./New York, established in 1972, has served as an indispensable cornerstone for not-for-profit theatre, supporting organizations from playwriting collectives to pioneering independent artists Art-newyorkArt-newyork. This production stands as proof of that mission’s ongoing relevance.

The intimate black-box space proves perfect for the production’s needs, creating a claustrophobic atmosphere that serves both the livestream conceit and the Gothic atmosphere. The audience becomes complicit witnesses, our proximity to the action eliminating the comfortable distance that traditional proscenium staging might provide.

Minor Reservations in a Major Achievement

If there are weaknesses in this otherwise exemplary production, they lie in occasional moments of meta-theatrical excess. The repeated references to livestreaming and social media, while thematically relevant, occasionally risk dating the material. Additionally, the play’s 90-minute runtime, while admirably economical, might benefit from slight expansion to allow specific philosophical arguments more breathing room.

Nevertheless, these are minor blemishes on what is fundamentally a work of theatrical excellence. Lynn has created a play that satisfies on multiple levels: as a Gothic thriller, a feminist manifesto, a philosophical inquiry, and pure theatrical entertainment. The work never loses sight of the theater’s dual obligation to instruct and delight, maintaining dramatic momentum even as it explores complex intellectual territory.

L-R: David Israeli. Courtesy davidisraeli.com. Miles Puriton, Courtesy milespuriton.com

Necessary for Our Times

The Truth About Transylvania stands as essential viewing for anyone invested in the future of American theater. The production’s partnership with the New York Blood Center for the October 29 performance adds a layer of civic engagement, transforming theatrical attendance into literal life-saving action—a gesture toward theater’s potential for genuine social impact.

In an era when truth itself has become contested terrain, Lynn’s play offers not answers but better questions. Moreover, it reminds us of that theater, at its finest, remains our most vital forum for collective interrogation of our deepest fears and most troubling certainties. The production asks us to consider not merely whether vampires exist, but what it means to believe, to testify, and to trust in an age of radical uncertainty.

As the lights fade on the ambiguous final tableau—a laugh echoing in darkness, a presence stepping into the room—we are left not with resolution but with productive disquiet. This is theater that follows you home, that whispers in the darkness, that makes you question the very ground beneath your feet. In other words, this is precisely the theater we need: provocative, intelligent, emotionally resonant, and unafraid to confront the monsters—both literal and metaphorical—that haunt our contemporary moment.

The Truth About Transylvania: A Gothic Triumph at the Mezzanine Theatre

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Little Engine Theater‘s mission is to find great plays from playwrights outside of the U.S, written or translated into English. They then look for a location that is not a typical theater situation and create a playing space.

For The Wasp, by Morgan Lloyd Malcolm (British playwright), Little Engine has found a loft space downtown in the financial district in a building scheduled to be torn down. They created a stage area in one corner of the space (beautifully designed by Scott Pask), put up some risers and chairs, and are presenting an absolute dynamite production of the play.

Two old secondary school friends connect up through Facebook twenty years later. Their lives are completely different, one with four kids, one on the way, not sure where the next rent payment is going to come from, and the other, worked her whole life to create a comfortable middle-class lifestyle. They both have buried pain from their school years, “That was 20 years ago. None of that stuff matters anymore.” But, “There is an impact to everything a person does,” and childhood actions create monstrous impact in their adult lives. One of them comes to the conversation with a hidden agenda that slowly gets revealed through surprising twists and turns eliciting audible gasps from the audience.

I’m kind of skirting around the plot as I don’t want to reveal too much and have it lose its powerful impact, but a key metaphor in the play is the tarantula hawk wasp that is pinned inside a picture frame mounted on the wall. A devastating (to a tarantula anyway) life-sucking bug that can only survive if the spider dies.

The Wasp is an intense psychological journey into the depths of festering childhood pain and disappointment that’s grown to become its own tumor in the adult. It will leave you at the edge of your seat as bits of personal histories divulge of who these women were twenty years ago and who they’ve become today.

This is one of those theatrical events where the writing, directing, acting, and design elements have all artfully coalesced to make theater what it can be at its finest.

Colby Minifie and Amy Forsyth, with the help of Rory McGregor‘s direction, are perfection in the characters they’ve created and deliver pitch-perfect performances. They give of themselves totally to the play, to themselves, and to the audience for their entertainment pleasure. Stacey Derosier‘s lighting and special effects lend themselves perfectly to the production, especially in this low ceiling space.

In one of my top ten productions for the year.

—–

The Wasp by Morgan Lloyd Malcolm and directed by Rory McGregor.

Starring: Colby Minifie and Amy Forsyth
Set Design by Scott Pask, Sound Design by Brian Hickey, Lighting Design by Stacey Derosier, Fight Choreography by Steve White, and Costume Design by Rodrigo Munoz.

Click HERE to purchase tickets. 90-minutes with no intermission.

General Admission: $38.43 – $59.23

Includes themes of trauma, bullying (including references to sexual assault), and scenes of a violent nature. There is also brief strobe lighting effects used during the performance.

By Paul Meltzer – Guest Contributor

First, the easy part.

This is a stunningly, compellingly performed show featuring the remarkable Jennifer Apple, bringing us through the inspiring life of a young woman we have heard far too little about.

Hannah Senesh was a promising high school student in Budapest in the 1930s who experiences the creep of rising, structural anti-Semitism and becomes more deeply involved in the Zionist youth movement.  She leaves her widowed mother (also portrayed by Ms. Apple with fierce commitment) in order to go to British Mandate Palestine to live and work on a kibbutz while studying agriculture, helping build a new country that will be a safe haven.  But as the Nazi noose tightens around her native Hungary, she feels compelled to find a way to go back, to fight alongside the partisans, and get more of her people out to safety.  She makes a thrilling, demanding, inspiring, and ultimately fateful choice to train and go back to Europe as a paratrooper under the British.

The style of the piece and of the performance actually reminds me of theater I’ve seen in Israel–crystal clear, a bit heightened and theatrical compared with New York Method’s utter naturalism, but played with complete emotional connection and commitment in every moment.  Nothing is tossed off or thrown away.  Everything counts, in a life and in a time when every choice mattered.

Ms. Apple brings us through every bit of it, fascinating to watch with her striking features and physical fearlessness, convincingly embodying every slight stage of maturation from the fifteen-year-old schoolgirl to the brave lioness at 22, not to mention the fully realized and entirely different Hungarian mother she portrays in two soliloquies. There is very clever and economical stagecraft, mostly executed through Designer Izzy Fields’ cleverly layered costuming–from an overly flouncy party dress to kibbutz-wear and then fighter gear.  The changes require no small bit of extra concentration by Ms. Apple to manage.  She doesn’t miss a beat. And with little more than a piece of cloth, she convinces us we now know what it feels like to parachute behind enemy lines.

Now the hard part.

The producers of this show, National Yiddishe Theatre Folkbiene, clearly feel a sense of mission to reach Jews and non-Jews alike with this distillation in one compelling life of the connection between anti-fascism and Zionism. Maybe it’s possible.  I am aware that compelling dramas can also be created around sympathetic individuals that would speak to audiences who would have entirely different reactions even to the words Zionism and Palestine.

If the producers can create greater understanding with this show, it can only be good.

 

 

Written and Directed by David Schechter

Starring Jennifer Apple

Presented in English by National Yiddish Theatre Folksbiene

Theatre Row, 410 W. 42nd Street, New York

Through Nov. 9

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

By Vicki Weisfeld

On stage just in time for Halloween and its otherworldly preoccupations is Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein at the Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey. Directed by the theater’s artistic director Brian B. Crowe, this haunting production (sorry!) opened October 25 and runs through November 16.

We’re familiar with the story of hubristic doctor Victor Frankenstein and his determination to create life. For two centuries, his experiment-gone-awry has prompted consideration of the limits of science, the difference between a man and a monster, and, in our current AI-obsessed era, what it means to be human. Astonishingly, Mary Shelley began writing this consequential story when she was only 18!

Author David Catlin frames Shelley’s story using the circumstances under which it was written. Mary was engaged in an affair with the married Percy Bysshe Shelley, and had borne him a daughter who died in infancy. The couple struggled financially and decamped to Geneva in 1816. That year, a huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia blackened skies worldwide. It was “the year without a summer.” Crops failed, livestock starved. In Switzerland, incessant rain. An uneasy time. They lived for a few months on Lake Geneva with poet Lord Byron, his physician, and Mary’s step-sister, Claire, Byron’s lover. To amuse themselves, they read and wrote ghost stories, and the result was not only Mary’s chilling tale but also John Polidori’s The Vampyre.

The STNJ cast takes on not only the roles of Shelley’s characters, but also the idle, somewhat bored, yet competitive authors. Actor Amber Friendly plays Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley (and Elizabeth); Sean-Michael Wilkinson is Shelley (and Victor Frankenstein); Jay Wade is Lord Byron (and the creature); and Brooke Turner is Claire (and Victor’s mother). The actors switch convincingly between these roles, with Neil Redfield (as Dr. Polidori and Henry and others) especially adept at immediately conveying different personas.

You cannot watch Wade’s athletic performance without sympathy for the creature’s yearning, his anger and confusion. Nor how Victor, preoccupied with his experiments, is heedless of their potential consequences, including how his monomania affects those he loves and denies him his own full humanity. Meanwhile, Elizabeth is a model of constancy in an uncertain world, hoping for but not expecting love. The story proceeds toward its tragic ending with the occasional intrusions by the poets and “real-life” characters, often foreshadowing their own fates. Women were not so simple, Mary believed, that they were free of dark impulses, and she proves it with her famous story.

STNJ has resisted the trend of providing patrons with a QR code instead of a printed program, and its nice biography of Mary Shelley is a thoughtful addition.

Production credits to Sarah Beth Hall (eerie set design), Andrew Hungerford (lightning effects and lighting design), Yao Chen (costumes, with the creature costume especially effective) and Ariana Cardoza (sound design; wow, the thunder!).

STNJ productions are hosted at Drew University in Madison, N.J. (easily reachable from NYC by train). For tickets, call the box office at 973-408-5600 or visit the Box Office online.

excerpt.rendered: Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein retells not just the familiar story by the personal and social context of how this remarkable story was written.

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

Confident productions, like confident people, succeed by taking risks. Beau: The Musical, an energetic, often touching one-act by Douglas Lyons and Ethan D. Pakchar, is a case in point. Following a brief, sold-out run at Theatre 154, the show has moved uptown to the tricky-to-configure space that is St. Luke’s Theatre. Under the assured direction of Josh Rhodes, the work establishes itself as both a memory play and a country-rock concert. The cast of eight are also the talented musicians who serve as the show’s band. And while coming-of-age stories are tried-and-true audience pleasers, rare is the tale that features a gay youth finding himself with the help of both a sexually confused bully and a gruff grandfather who extols the healing power of music.

When we first meet Ace Baker (Matt Rodin), the show’s protagonist, lead singer, and narrator, he too is confident. His band’s latest album is about to debut, and the group is performing at their favorite honky-tonk in his hometown of Nashville. But it was a long road to success, as we learn when Ace opens up the journals he kept as a kid and flashes back to his troubled adolescent days.

Ace never knew his father, who split before he was born, leaving him to be raised by his empowering, if overprotective, mother, Raven (Amelia Cormack). His desire for a male role model is palpable, and one falls into his lap when he answers the phone one day. It’s a nurse in Memphis calling to say that Beau (Jeb Brown), his grandfather, has been hospitalized. This is especially newsworthy for Ace because, as far as he knew, he had no relatives other than his mom.

Why Raven had kept her son unaware of her own father is one of several secrets that are slowly revealed, but not before Ace and Beau bond, with Raven keeping her distance but allowing Ace to spend summers with him over the following years. Beau, a former rocker himself with a band called the Bell Bottoms (“We just knew we were real good, but lookin’ back at it we were just real drunk”) teaches Ace to play guitar while his problems back in Nashville intensify. Not only has Raven taken up with Larry, a Ned Flanders-esque boyfriend (Ryan Halsaver), but Ace’s relationship with his classmate Ferris (Max Sangerman) has grown ever more complex.

When they were twelve, Ferris was a violent bully who, when dealing with Ace, didn’t know whether to punch him or kiss him. So he did both. The resulting years of secret liaisons for Ace confirmed his sexuality, while for Ferris, they led to denial, which ultimately turned to disgust. In the show’s strongest musical number, the two consider their passions in the duet “It Couldn’t Be,” singing, “I’m open for you/I could explore you/Is that a crime?”

Rodin is charismatic as Ace, and the chemistry with Brown’s sensitive interpretation of Beau grounds the play nicely. Rounding out the cast, Miyuki Miyagi is Ace’s closest friend, Daphney. It’s an underwritten role, but Miyagi’s fine fiddle playing is an essential element. Andrea Goss is unloved twice, as both Ferris’s girlfriend and Beau’s ex-wife. And percussionist Derek Stoltenberg steps out from behind his plexiglass cage to drum up Beau’s soft side.

Scenic designer Daniel Allen tries to solve the problems of the square-shaped, unraked theatre space by creating three separate playing areas: a small, functional bar that serves double duty as a bathroom stall, a tiny, raised circular stage in the center of the house, and a larger upstage platform where the full band can rock out. This means a lot of neck-turning for the audience, who sit inside and outside the action while the actors dash about. It is also a tough task for lighting designer Japhy Weideman, who must illuminate multiple playing spaces from a low ceiling. I had the unique treat of being temporarily blinded from three different directions over the course of the night.

 

Beau The Musical – By Douglas Lyons, directed and choreographed by Josh Rhodes,  music by Ethan D. Pakchar and Douglas Lyons.

WITH: Matt Rodin (Ace Baker), Jeb Brown (Beau), Amelia Cormack (Raven ), Andrea Goss ( Le-Ann/Karina/Nurse), Miyuki Miyagi (Daphney ), Derek Stoltenberg (Dennis), Ryan Halsaver (Larry) and Max Sangerman (Ferris).

Chris Gurr (Music Supervisor), Daniel Allen (Scenic Designer), Rodrigo Muñoz (Costume Designer), Japhy Weideman (Lighting Designer), Jordana Abrenica (Sound Designer). The Distillery at St. Luke’s Theatre, 308 West 46th St., beauthemusical.com. Through December 7. Running time: 100 minutes

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

…Happy is for the victim that chooses victory.

A generational family home, in southern Mississippi, is battered and worn. “It’s a cursed house. Not by design, but by decision.”

A BBQ brings Keyshawn–played by Jordan E. Cooper, writer of OH HAPPY DAY!–wearing Gucci and bedazzled jeans, to the front porch. Seeing himself as a “thick ass blotchy black stain,” Keyshawn is returning home for something. It’s the birthday of Lewis (Brian D. Coats): Keyshawn and Niecy’s (Tamika Lawrence) father, but Lewis is reluctant to celebrate with cake and balloons. 

Photo by Joan Marcus

Keyshawn, a male prostitute, has been kicked out of the home but we are left wondering for more than half the play what the circumstances are surrounding this conflict. When we find out the dark truth alongside the family, the audience audibly feels the same tremendous sadness and shock.

The specific familial relationships weren’t immediately clear between Lewis, Keyshawn, Niecy, and the previous mother figures living in the home.

Niecy’s son, Kevin (Donovan Louis Bazemore), is their hope for a better future.

But, Keyshawn–whether in the flesh or not–is commanded to build an ark; hence, we are about to watch a modern and literal calling to spiritually save himself and his family. This house “peeling with pain” becomes a place of refuge, it’s an ark to weather a storm, it’s the gateway to heaven.

Keyshawn needs to prove to God that this house belongs to him. One of my favorite aspects of this place, in a religious standpoint, was that I sat there wondering why or how the house could belong to him, as if his name was on the deed, or it had been willed to him–but really, I began to understand that that house symbolized God’s kingdom.

This piece highlights how we are all fallen and flawed. The most memorable parts of this production are when each character embodies God, and He shines through—metaphorically, physically–both. 

The Divine’s. Photo by Joan Marcus.

The house is not just a place to sleep, it’s a place of refuge, it’s an ark to weather their storm, it’s the gateway to heaven. But those blue painted panels are “peeling with pain.”

God has spoken to Keyshawn, giving him the opportunity to come forward with his truth to his family, to repair their relationship, and to make peace. To be happy. If Keyshawn can build an ark to cast them to safety when a storm comes, he’ll be able to come home. He will find for what he’s spent his entire life searching: Happy.

OH HAPPY DAY! is a whirlwind of emotions; I’m laughing one moment after another line of Jordan E. Cooper hilarious references: I’m thinking he went there. And the next I’m wiping my nose. While the shift in tones is jolting, I have nothing but praise for its intensity and effectiveness. The depth of this production deepens significantly after intermission. Suddenly purses are dropping, people are thumbing for tissues, a group of women behind me is sniffling, the man next to me has tears rolling down his cheeks, and so do I. 

This is church; maybe the most straight forward and communal service I have ever attended. From the roof, Niecy delivers a sermon. From the windows, Kevin reminds us we’re in control of our Happy, not our life. The voices of The Divine’s–a narrative and uplifting chorus–deliver us to Mississippi, drop us into conversations with God, and take us home.

This production is a bit niche, but I also recommend everyone to run to this show. It’s impressive in its ability to connect. It’s not just me—this audience was PRESENT. A congregation clapping and acknowledging the conversations, arguments, monologues and the gospel sprinkled through song and narrative.

Whether you are religious or not, I think this play absolutely resonates with everyone. If you understand the self Keyshawn presents to the audience–Christianity set aside–we see a man searching for happiness after a life of trauma, lies, and hiding. We realize that we may not know what even those closest to us have been through, and it’s important to give people the time, space, and energy to simply be kind and listen.

When I stepped outside post show, I had to take deep breaths. So much feeling that hit, really hard.

A monster ain’t nothing but somebody tryna be bigger than the pain yelling inside of ’em.

Written by Jordan E. Cooper and directed by Stevie Walker-Webb. Original Songs by Donald Lawrence.

CAST: Donovan Louis Bazemore (Kevin), Brian D. Coats (Lewis), Jordan E. Cooper (Keyshawn), Tamika Lawrence (Niecy), Tiffany Mann (Holy Divine), Sheléa Melody McDonald (Mighty Divine), Latrice Pace (Glory Divine), and Cole Taylor (Understudy), Jayna Elise (Understudy).

CREATIVE TEAM: Luciana Stecconi (Scenic Design), Qween Jean (Costume Design), Adam Honoré (Lighting Design), Taylor J. Williams (Sound Design), Mia Neal (Hair and Wig Design), Kirk Cambridge Del-Pesche (Makeup Design), Samantha Llanes Gordon (Prop Management), Eboni Nichols (Choreography), Jack Phillips Moore (Dramaturgy), Sara Jacovino and KristyNorter (Music Contracting), Daniel Rudin (Music Direction/Supervision/Orchestration/Additional Music).

OH HAPPY DAY! is presented in Association with Baltimore Center Stage and has been extended to run until Nov. 9, 2025 at The Public Theater, Martinson Hall, with a runtime of 2 hours and 10 minutes, including one intermission. Tickets can be purchased here.

It’s not just me—this audience was PRESENT. A congregation clapping and acknowledging the conversations, arguments, monologues and the gospel sprinkled through song and narrative.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

A little over twenty years ago I saw a production of “Endgame” at the Matrix Theatre in L.A.  It was directed by Andrew Robinson and the cast I saw (they rotated) featured Robin Gammell as Hamm, Allan Arbus as Nagg, Claudette Sutherland as Nell and Cotter Smith as Clov.

I don’t know why or how it happened, but that production was the first time I felt keyed in to Beckett.  It seemed that this production revealed Beckett’s intention – to examine time.  To pull it apart the way a scientist pulls apart an insect under a microscope.  Robinson’s direction was crystal clear and the performances were without embellishment, leaving the characters and the story free to wander through our minds.

What I learned from that 1995 production still holds, and this production of “Endgame” is a welcome place to visit. No matter the bleak setting of the tale.  This “Endgame” is worth the trip  to the Irish Arts Center located on the far reaches of the West Side. The very far reaches.

This production of Endgame comes to us from Galway’s Druid, a touring theater company that was founded 50 years ago.  Garry Hynes, this production’s director, was one of the founding members.  An interview with her and one of the other co-founders, Marie Mullen, can be found here.

“Endgame” is an investigation into an ending that is promised but never arrives.  Despite the protestations of Hamm (Rory Nolan) who is central to the staging as well as the story.  The endgame is upon us (in case you had forgotten) but the end is still elusive.  In the mean time we are invited to watch the few people left on earth while away the minutes that are never ending, until they amount to something that is an ending.

Grain upon grain, one by one, and one day, suddenly, there’s a heap, a little heap, the impossible heap.

Watching gains of time accumulate is not as boring as it may sound.  Each moment is a small combustible engine that fires off every few seconds as if Beckett is testing to see if we are paying attention.  Hamm is a decaying leftover of a man who now has only his manservant Clov (Aaron Monaghan) whose main job is to remind Hamm that life IS happening.

ENDGAME: Aaron Monaghan and Rory Nolan; Photo by HanJie Chow

The two are paired by disabilities.  Hamm cannot walk and Clove cannot sit.  Hamm cannot see what is on the other side of the elevated dungeon windows (kudos to Francis O’Connor and James F. Ingalls for set and lighting design respectively) that transform into the eyes of the world as we watch.  Clov can and chooses to look out the windows at Hamm’s command and narrates the slow demise of the world he sees.

In addition to this pair are Hamm’s parents, Mother (Marie Mullen) and Father (Bosco Hogan) neatly contained in two trash-bins.  These two only appear when called, and their presence gives us the proof that Hamm was once more than what he is presently.  The storage place for the parents seems logical – who hasn’t considered the same idea?  Anyone?

ENDGAME: Bosco Hogan and Marie Mullen; HanJie Chow

This foursome plays a slow but intriguing game of something-or-other.  Lines are tossed, caught and returned.  Each syllable, each motion, each subtle change of light in this dungeon are handed out judiciously because each is a full blown sphere holding a universe.  The words connect like a chain link fence. Little by little, this most excellent ensemble delivers up the grains of the tale without hesitating or letting any single one drop until, voilà – we come round to the place where we began.

Life is not linear.  It is circular.  Watch  your back.

ENDGAME by Samuel Beckett’s Endgame, directed by Garry Hynes

WITH Aaron Monaghan as Clov, Rory Nolan as Hamm, Marie Mullen as Nell, and Bosco Hogan as Nagg.

The creative team includes Francis O’Connor (Set and Costume Designer), James F. Ingalls(Lighting Designer), Gregory Clarke(Sound Designer), Gráinne Coughlan(Hair and Make-Up Designer), and Clíodhna Hallissey (Associate Costume Designer

Through November 23 at the Irish Arts Center, 726 11th Ave at 51st Street.  TICKETS HERE.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: American Lyric Theater’s Luminous Anniversary Gala

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Tonight was a celebration of  20 years of vision, artistry, and the transformative power of new opera.

With inspired comments and introductions from ALT founder Lawrence Edelson, Thursday evening at Merkin Hall offered more than just a concert—it delivered a revelation. American Lyric Theater‘s twentieth anniversary gala demonstrated with unmistakable clarity why sustained artistic mentorship matters, why the patient cultivation of creative partnerships yields extraordinary fruit, and why the future of American opera burns so brightly. The atmosphere crackled with anticipation as audience members gathered to witness not merely performances but a living testament to two decades of transformative work in the operatic arts.

L-R: Susan Feder. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR, Royce Vavrek, Librettist. Courtesy roycevaverek.com, Lawrence Edelson. Founder, Artistic Director, and General Director of American Lyric Theater. Courtesy altnyc.org

One thinks of Leonard Bernstein‘s celebrated observation that “music can name the unnameable and communicate the unknowable”—and indeed, throughout this evening’s extraordinary showcase of contemporary American opera, we witnessed precisely such feats of artistic alchemy, as the fruits of ALT’s pioneering Composer Librettist Development Program demonstrated the profound depths to which collaboration between words and music can illuminate the human condition.

The Visionary Foundation: Honoring Susan Feder

The evening featured a well-deserved tribute to Susan Feder, whose fifteen-year tenure as a program officer at the Mellon Foundation proved instrumental—one might say indispensable—to ALT’s evolution from a modest startup into a premier cultural incubator. Feder spoke with characteristic elegance about the newly established fellowship bearing her name, her words suffused with the rare wisdom she had gleaned over decades of nurturing artistic excellence. Moreover, her presence reminded us that great operas, as ALT’s tagline rightfully proclaims, genuinely don’t just happen—they require visionaries who understand that the future of opera depends not merely on commissions and productions, but on the sustained development of the artists who create them.

L-R: Jonathan Michie, Baritone. Karen Vuong, Soprano, Justin Hopkins, Bass Baritone. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

Cultivating Tomorrow’s Masterworks: The CLDP Legacy

At the heart of this celebration stood the remarkable legacy of the Composer Librettist Development Program (CDL),  America’s only full-time professional mentorship initiative for operatic writers. Furthermore, the evening’s centerpiece revelation—a preview of “Dear Little Chap” from Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek‘s Lincoln in the Bardo—served as a luminous testament to the program’s efficacy.

Varek was on hand to speak about the commission by The Metropolitan Opera for its anticipated 2026 world premiere of Lincoln in the Bardo. The Met’s upcoming performance of this work represents a watershed moment: the first opera by a CLDP alumna to grace the hallowed stage of America’s premier opera house. Vavrek spoke eloquently of his formative years in the program, his remarks illuminating the profound impact of ALT’s unique pedagogical approach—one that treats librettists and composers as equal collaborators in the sacred act of operatic creation.

A Tapestry of American Voices

The evening’s program traversed an impressive panorama of contemporary operatic achievement, each excerpt offering its own distinctive contribution to the evolving canon of American opera.

From Jeremy Howard Beck and Stephanie Fleischmann‘s emotionally searing The Long Walk—based on Brian Castner‘s haunting memoir—to Derrick Wang‘s witty Scalia/Ginsburg and Jasmine Arielle Barnes and Deborah D.E.E.P. Mouton‘s She Who Dared, the selections revealed the remarkable breadth of ALT’s artistic vision.

Works like Christopher Cerrone and Tony Asaro‘s All Wounds Bleed and Aleksandra Vrebalov and Deborah Brevoort‘s The Knock demonstrated how contemporary opera can engage with urgent social and political questions.

At the same time, Ricky Ian Gordon and Royce Vavrek‘s The House Without A Christmas Tree and Alex Weiser and Stephanie Fleischmann‘s Tevye’s Daughters explored the timeless territories of family, memory, and belonging.

L-R: Andrew Bidlack, Tenor, Caroline Worra, Soprano. Ethan Vincent. Baritone. Photos courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

The assembled artists brought these diverse works to vivid life with consistently impressive artistry. Baritones Jonathan Michie and Gideon Dabi navigated complex emotional terrain with remarkable nuance, while mezzo-sopranos Heather Johnson and Gina Perregrino brought depth and color to their respective roles. Tenor Andrew Bidlack‘s clarion sound and bass-baritone Justin Hopkins’ commanding presence added further luster to the proceedings. Soprano Karen Vuong demonstrated exceptional versatility across multiple selections, while Jacqueline Echols McCarley’s dramatic intensity proved particularly striking in excerpts from She Who Dared. Soprano Jennifer Zetlan distinguished herself with coloratura passages of crystalline precision and an interpretive depth that brought particular warmth to both the virtuosic demands of Scalia/Ginsburg and the poignant lyricism of Tevye’s Daughters. Soprano Caroline Worra and baritone Ethan Vincent rounded out this stellar ensemble with performances of consummate professionalism.

The Collaborative Spirit: Musical Leadership and Artistic Excellence

The evening’s pianists—Djordje Nesic, Kelly Kuo, and Jason Wirth—deserved special commendation for their sensitive and virtuosic accompaniments. These accomplished musicians served not merely as accompanists but as true collaborative partners, their playing revealing the intricate musical architecture of each work while supporting the vocalists with unwavering sensitivity. Their contribution exemplified the collaborative ethos that has defined ALT’s approach from its inception—the recognition that grand opera emerges not from individual genius alone, but from the confluence of many artistic streams flowing toward a shared vision.

Artistic Faith and Vision

Opera has always been the most complete of artistic expressions—a convergence of music, drama, visual spectacle, choreography, and narrative that creates something greater than the sum of its parts. In the nineteenth century, audiences entered opera houses seeking precisely this kind of total immersion, an opportunity to suspend disbelief and inhabit worlds both fantastical and profoundly human. Each listener brought their own understanding to the unfolding story, making the experience simultaneously collective and deeply personal. Today, while technological innovations offer new possibilities for spectacle and scenic transformation, opera’s essential power remains rooted in something far more elemental: the dedicated artistry of singers, instrumentalists, dancers, visual artists, and creators who devote their lives to mastering this demanding craft. It is this human dimension—the voice that can convey joy and anguish in a single phrase, the composer who labors to capture an ineffable emotion in notation, the librettist who finds the precise words to unlock meaning—that continues to make opera uniquely capable of piercing through our contemporary distractions to touch something essential in the human spirit.

Gideon Babi, Baritone. Courtesy gideonbabi.com. Jennifer Zetlan, Soprano. Courtesy jenniferzetlan.com

As the evening drew to its post-champagne-toasted denouement, one reflected on the profound significance of what Lawrence Edelson and his colleagues have achieved over these two decades. Like the great impresarios of opera’s golden age—yet working within distinctly contemporary circumstances—ALT has created an institution that nurtures productions and artists, not spectacles but sustainable artistic collaborations. The result is a body of work that has already begun to enrich the operatic repertoire, with ALT alums’s compositions performed by more than 125 companies worldwide.

In this age when so much of our cultural discourse centers on preservation and nostalgia, American Lyric Theater reminds us that the operatic tradition remains vital precisely because it continues to evolve, to embrace new voices and new stories, to find fresh ways of articulating those essential human truths that transcend any single era or aesthetic. As we departed into the October evening, the melodies and words of this remarkable program still resonating in our consciousness, we carried with us not merely memories of beautiful performances but renewed faith in opera’s capacity to surprise, to challenge, and to illuminate the depths of human experience.

L-R Jacqueline Echols, Soprano. Heather Johnson, Mezzo Soprano. Gina Perregrino, Mezzo Soprano. Photos courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

content.rendered:
By David Walters

 

“When you are not fed love on a silver spoon, you learn to lick it off of knives.” – poet Lauren Eden

Everyone has their own idea of what love is. Their love language. What makes them feel seen, heard, and safe.

Ones’ love language is expressed in many different ways, from the kind that wraps you like a warm blanket right out of the dryer, to the kind that inflicts physical and psychological harm in order to toughen up a person for the cruel world. All given and inflicted out of “love.”

Zoë Kim grew up with the latter. Her journey that brought her to The Public’s Shiva Theater stage has been her searching for the former. What she shares with the audience is her revolution, her journey, her voyage into self and what she needs as an adult that she didn’t get as a child.

It is so very difficult to change who we are, to morph into someone else beyond what our parents and our upbringing have endowed us with, to change and learn how to love ourselves. Psychologists and meditation gurus purport that is our only true goal in life. Zoë does that every night of this production. By sharing her journey and you witnessing it, there may be hope for us all.

The title, DID YOU EAT? (밥 먹었니?), comes from suppressed meanings of Zoë’s mother’s inability to say what she was truly feeling. Instead of, “I’m worried about you,” “I’m sorry,” or “How are you?” she would use a rendition of, “Did you eat?” to express that feeling.

We often give to others from our love language even though the person we’re giving to doesn’t speak our dialect, much less our language of love. If we don’t take the time to figure out what language the other person speaks, we may never be able to communicate in any worthwhile way. Misunderstandings all around.

I really can’t say that this is a Korean/American story and what struck me in my heart is that it is a human story first. What Zoe experienced in her life translates to anywhere on this earth where we humans tred. The autobiographical journey that Zoë takes her audience on is as much a dance as it is a telling. Zoë’s graceful movements, with intricate choreography by Iris McCloughan, creates a unique presentation that allows some of the pressure of childhood trauma to escape and gives the audience a chance to breathe. The projections by Yee Eun Nam and lighting by Minjoo Kim act as music accompaniment to the piece adding to the tensions and highlighting the different moods and movements as the play progresses.

What you come out with after the show is over is the personal strength of Zoë Kim. Her life could have broken a person with lesser conviction and as she plunges down the rabbit hole of her life’s journey and a respect for human endurance. Zoe’s journey to love through her life is pretty horrific. She has come to a place of self-respect and growth that was absent from the beginning. this presentation is cathartic for her, and brave, and riveting, and hopefully reflects back on you and the choices you’ve made in your life, surrounding what love is to you and those close to you.

Love each other.

—–
DID YOU EAT? (밥 먹었니?) was written and performed by Zoë Kim. Directed by Chris Yejin. Choreographed by Iris McCloughan.

Scenic design by Tanya Orellana, costume design by Harriet Jung, lighting design by Minjoo Kim, sound design by Tae Jong Park, projection design by Yee Eun Nam, dramaturgy by Amrita Ramanan,

Tickets can be accessed by visiting publictheater.org, calling 212.967.7555, or in person at the Taub Box Office at The Public Theater at 425 Lafayette Street through Sunday, November 16.
Running time is 70 minutes with no intermission
Triggers: the play addresses complex and sensitive topics including experiences of childhood trauma, self-harm, and suicidal ideation.

By David Walters

Now through November 2 at Soho Playhouse, the solo comedy show Unstuck  is entertaining audiences with a mashup of the manifestations of OCD and the self-discovery of being queer. This being akin to riding Steel Vengeance at Cedar Point (world’s wildest roller coaster), upside down. Expect things to come out of all orifices.

OCD, though often misunderstood, is a chronic mental health condition that can become all-encompassing and take over someone’s life to the extent that they see themselves and everyone around them only through this lens. It focuses on the things that the person cares most about, and laser beams a false sense of power over them.

Olivia Levine tells her raw and honest story of growing up, finding out who she is, and learning to become unstuck in her life. This wild ride through her life is both entertaining and horrifying at the same time.in her sharing that brings about an understanding and a comradery. Is it the constant laughs? Is it her disarmingly inviting smile?

I used the word raw earlier because in Unstuck she shares the true depths of her OCD, how it manifests itself, and how she has figured out how to move in this world saddled with the compulsions that overtake her. In revealing herself, she, metaphorically, not only takes off her clothes for us to see the real her, but sheds her skin, reaches deeper inside and cracks her ribs open so we can see the guts of who she is. Cringy sometimes, yes. But much more than brave on her part revealing her most private moments in such an open way. What makes it work and keeps us from turning away and keeps this show from being a traumalogue, is her personal charm and her great gift to be able to laugh at herself, causing the audience to laugh along with her. A priceless gift. She has an open and inviting personality that makes you want to keep your eyes wide-open as she strips herself of all the veneer that we humans usually shelter ourselves with.

Revealing her awareness of her sexuality and how that did and did not translate to having a relationship, her obsession with masturbation, her fixation on preventing her parents from dying, she invites us to share in her self-realization. She does this symbolically at the top of the show by sharing her orange(s) with the audience. A nice way to build immediate rapport. To keep it throughout the show, she’s just herself, her complete self, and the audience loves her for it.

—–

Unstuck, written and performed by Olivia Levine and directed by Molly Rose Heller.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

The show has a running time of 60 minutes and is recommended for 18+ audiences.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Every season there’s one or two shows that are just too painful to sit through.

Unfortunately, Art of Leaving is one of those.

And I’m not saying the performance itself was of poor quality; the cast was fine. Rather, it was the show’s presentation of masculinity–

Art of Leaving, written by Anne Marilyn Lucas and directed by Matt Gehring, examines what a marriage can be through different generations and the decisions that will literally break or continue the relationship. Though in either situation, there seems to be at least one person disappointed. The piece opens in an extremely clean, organized, and gray apartment where Aaron (Jordan Lage) and Diana (Audrey Heffernan Meyer) reside together. It actually reminds me of the set for a sit-com. Aaron’s flexing in front of a mirror, lecturing his wife on how to properly prepare his health smoothies, and rebuking her decision to buy him turkey instead of chicken. Is this a midlife crisis or honestly a huge flaw of Aaron? Because I sense that he’s always been this insecure, self-centered, finicky man.

I wonder if Aaron and Diana are a new couple, a one-night stand, or newly married. I would not have guessed they were about to celebrate their twentieth-fifth wedding anniversary, but, maybe this is intentional.

Aaron is obsessed with a men’s self-help guru who seemingly does not support anything that could potentialy diminish an ounce of a man’s masculinity. Aaron treats this man as a prophet, his book Male Satisfaction Over 40 as a gift from above, and fully subscribes to him to a very, very unhealthy level. While this is clear to the audience, I expected this to become a hot topic in Aaron and Diana’s marriage, but instead the guru’s teachings became motivation for Aaron decide whether this marriage was really satisfying him. 

While Diana continues through her day at work, I feel a bit of sympathy for her but disgusted that she has allowed this man who physically pounds self-affirmations into his chest in front of a mirror to be such a commanding figure in her life. The contrast of this 50-year old man ridiculously controlling his wife with their son (Brian Mason) and his fiancé (Molly Chiffer) is laughable but also realistic in this day and age. This young couple in their 20’s are navigating a relationship that’s one-sided in a desire for a poly-amorous marriage. Cue the addition of Aaron’s parents, Esther (Pamela Shaw) and Felix (Alan Ceppos) to the living room, and we have a whole family who are unsatisfied in their relationships but think they know what is best for Aaron and Diana.

The old-school stereotypes that fly out of Esther’s mouth make the audience groan, and it’s a bit much that I’m also shifting in my seat, uncomfortable. Whether the middle-aged and older singles and married couples in the audience surrounding me connected to this or not, the dialogue was a lot. An embarrassing level of masculine stereotyping takes over Aaron and the appropriateness that Esther and Diana find in their husbands hurt.

These three generations come together, in Aaron’s living room, when Aaron drops a bombshell on his wife, Diana. We wonder if Diana will be strong enough to make a decision that prioritizes her own self-satisfaction and happiness, or if the couple will work out their gripes with identity and self-worth in this seemingly love-less marriage.

Ultimately, every stereotype of aging men, midlife crises, and couple conflicts are referenced on stage. It was like there was a checklist of clichés, stereotypical lines to say that would make the audience hate men and the relationship dynamics of those in their 20’s and those in their 50’s alike.

I would give this one big cringe.

Written by Anne Marilyn Lucas; directed by Matt Gehring.

STARRING: Audrey Heffernan Meyer (Diana), Jordan Lage (Aaron), Alan Ceppos (Felix), Pamela Shaw (Esther), Molly Chiffer (Caitlyn), and Brian Mason (Jason).

CREATIVE TEAM: Dan Hasse (Dramaturg), Frank Oliva (Scenic Designer), Lara De Bruijn (Costume Designer), Kevin Foster (Wig Designer), Betsy Chester (Lighting Designer), and Ben Vigus (Sound Designer).

Art of Leaving is playing Off-Broadway at The Alice Griffin Jewel Box Theatre, The Pershing Square Signature Center, 480 West 42nd Street,  New York. Art of Leaving is not a Signature production.

Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

You only have a few more opportunities to see “Adam Gopnik’s New York”, (it closes on the 26th) billed as a “theatrical event” which is an honest appraisal.  This is not a one-person show as we think of them.  A one-person show implies that the person on the stage is an actor.  Gopnik is not an actor.  He is an extraordinary writer and observer who has found in his home town plenty to observe.

Gopnik is a jewel of a writer. He drifts from subject to subject  as if he were reading from a book of his own essays.  Within each story there is a beginning, middle and end.  He goes deep where most of us would pass by the subject on our way to one thing or another.

Did you know that Olmsted designed Central Park as a social project?  Its purpose was the coming together of people for the “practice of pleasure” – which was an extraordinary idea wrapped up in nature.  Politics, social standing, money or the lack thereof would divide us, but in Central Park our common shared goal was pleasure.  Gopnik tells us the park is his political philosophy.

There is the story of the story of “Proust and the Sex Rats” – no more needed there.

He explains his article “Quattrocento Baseball” that attempted to work out his profession as an art critic and student of fifteenth-century Italian art and also being fan of the Montreal Expos.

Did you know that snowflakes start out their lives as identical entities?  It is only through their journey to earth that they are reshaped into the individual objects they become.  Huh.  Kind of like life wouldn’t you say?

Snowflakes? Not something most of us talked about until Gopnik put it in our sight lines.

Joseph Mitchell, who had been at the New Yorker nearly 50 years by the time Gopnik arrived in 1986, said that the best writers had a “wild exactitude” in their work.  This phrase became a benchmark for Gopnik.  His writing mightily succeeds and this event comes close to Mitchell’s ideal.

And that is how the event rolls out.  One essay after another strung together by the teller.  There is no director listed, and that is the one thing this writer would suggest.  Gopnik puts enormous pressure on himself by memorizing 90 minutes worth of thoughtful writing.  It would be just as compelling if he read it.  As it is, his pauses are often distracting and lack specificity.  I wondered more than once if he had forgotten his line or could not decide what story would be next.

As he tells us from the beginning – he is not something you can move past by swiping.  He is a three dimensional being – as are we all.  Next time out (and I hope there is one) I hope he gets the stage guidance that his writing deserves.

Adam Gopnik’s New York Producers: Steve Martin and James L. Nederlander

The autobiographical solo show will play October 17-26 at The Clark Studio Theater at Lincoln Center (Samuel B. & David Rose Building, 165 West 65th Street).  Tickets are now on sale HERE.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.
